news.title: Fast Takes: Leave the theatrics to Hollywood, Dems outgrew common sense and more
news.text:
Democrat: Leave the Theatrics to Hollywood

The US entertainment industry’s “gloriously cutthroat” spirit “makes America the cultural center of the world and a domestic economic growth engine,” but the suit by a dozen blue-state attorneys general to “block the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance puts it all at risk” with bogus antitrust claims, warns Ari Emanuel at The Wall Street Journal. In their “trash” antitrust case, the AGs “pretend Amazon MGM, A24 and Lionsgate don’t exist” though their films have grossed billions already this year. The merged firm’s “27% share of feature-film box office” won’t “substantially lessen competition”; indeed, the deal leaves the new company “committed to at least 30 theatrical releases a year.” “The harm doesn’t begin when the attorneys general win their suit,” it began when money started to pour “into legal fees rather than productions.” “Let Hollywood creatives get back to trying to rip each other’s heads off . . . it’s what we’re best at.”

Conservative: Dems Outgrew Common Sense

Elon Musk in a recent interview offered “a powerful diagnosis of the growing gulf between America and Europe, Republicans and Democrats, ‘normal people’ and the mainstream media,” remarks USA Today’s Nicole Russell. The interviewer claimed Musk “supports not just the populist right but the far right — in fact, very fringe parties”; he replied, “No, I support the normal people. What you call the far right, falsely.” Russell continues: He dared his questioner “to consider that 10 to 15 years ago, Obama and Clinton held the same views on immigration and other issues that Trump holds today, views the ‘lunatic left’ now brands far right.” At every level of government, “commonsense ideas Democrats once agreed on are now dismissed as fringe” and: “The chasm between right and left” is “dug deeper by the media.”

Libertarian: Too Many Elex Over From the Start

Some 150 House races this year “had no meaningful competition,” gripes Reason’s Eric Boehm, with incumbents “all but guaranteed another two years in office after running unopposed in their primaries” in districts that are super-safe red or blue seats — leaving more than 84 million Americans “effectively disenfranchised.” California, Washington and Hawaii now have “open, all-candidate primaries,” leaving only five of their 63 House seats uncontested. Yes, that often means “two candidates from the same party advancing” to the general, but it beats watching more than one-third of candidates win before the election even starts. “Americans should be embracing any and all ideas that aim to make elections more competitive.”

Historian: DSA Takeover Was By Invitation

The socialist “takeover of the Democratic Party” wasn’t sparked by concerns about ‘affordability,’ ” but “was merely the logical culmination of . . . radicalism within the Democratic aristocracy,” including “Elizabeth Warren, Kamala Harris, and Hakeem Jeffries,” contends Victor Davis Hanson at American Greatness. “Mainstream Democrats” spread nearly every “weaponized scam and national hysteria in the last two decades.” Did the “Democratic apparat calm the waters,” when “three would-be assassins got close enough to killing Trump?” Did they “at least pretend to deplore the violence” against ICE? No, socialists “did not hijack the party;” they “were spawned and nurtured by aged Democrats,” adding only antisemitism. “America will soon see how this insanity works out.”

Urbanist: Rent Freeze at Real Risk

In response to the Rent Guidelines Board vote “to fulfill the mayor’s campaign promise” of a “rent freeze,” a group of “affected property owners” have sued “to nullify” that 0% hike, notes City Journal’s John Ketcham. A politically-motivated vote “could constitute a violation of due process.” The law requires the RGB to “weigh evidence of certain economic factors” in its deliberations, yet the “evidence before the RGB — based upon the board’s own research — does not support” the freeze, since it found landlords’ expenses up 5.3% in the last year. Plus, multiple board members have well-documented “histories of anti-owner bias,” also supporting “a finding that the RGB’s decision was arbitrary and capricious.”

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board
news.summary: The Wall Street Journal's Ari Emanuel slams the lawsuit blocking the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger, while NYC landlords sue to nullify a rent freeze.

news.title: Trump rejected $227m in disaster relief to blue states after FEMA OK’d the money
news.text:
President Trump reportedly rejected $227 million in disaster aid requests this month from four Democrat-led states, despite federal disaster officials certifying that damage in these areas hit established thresholds to trigger federal aid.

In the wake of a record-setting snowstorm that hit the East Coast in February, New Jersey, New York, Massachusetts and Rhode Island sought federal assistance.

Regional offices of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration affirmed the extent of the need in New Jersey, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, according to documents obtained by Politico, while officials in New York told the outlet they also had a request rejected despite administration officials allegedly concluding it met federal standards.

In one alleged example, FEMA's New England office certified more than $19 million of damages in Rhode Island, more than nine times FEMA's usual cost threshold for the state.

President Trump still rejected the request despite this analysis, a highly unusual move, according to disaster experts.

"I can't think of a time a declaration was denied," a former FEMA official told Politico.

The Independent has contacted the White House and NOAA for comment.

"FEMA assesses a number of factors to determine the severity, magnitude, and impact of a disaster event," the agency told The Independent. "Major disaster declaration request evaluation factors considered include estimated cost of the assistance, localized impacts, insurance coverage in force, hazard mitigation, recent multiple disasters, programs of other federal assistance, state fiscal capacity and resource availability, uninsured home and personal property losses, disaster-impacted population profile, impact to community infrastructure, casualties, and disaster related unemployment."

It declined to comment on whether the president had rejected any of its analyses about the snowstorm.

The Trump administration has denied political favoritism played into the July aid decision, which came two days after President Trump approved disaster aid to six Republican-led states. (In general, the president has approved nearly 90 percent of requests from states governed by members of his party, more than three times the rate of approvals for Democrat-led states, Politico previously found.)

Since the George W. Bush administration, presidents have approved all but one request for snow aid that meets FEMA standards, according to a recent analysis.

Last week, more than a dozen states sued the Trump administration, arguing it was wrongly trying to tie election and immigration policy demands to federal disaster aid.

The Trump administration has scoffed at the suit, calling it "partisan pushback" against "commonsense measures" from "leftwing politicians."

The Trump administration initially toyed with eliminating FEMA, though a Trump-backed review council recommended earlier this year that the agency instead share more work with state and local governments while streamlining its processes.

Lawmakers are considering a bipartisan bill to elevate FEMA from its place inside the Department of Homeland Security to an independent, Cabinet-level agency, while expediting payments to survivors.

The Trump administration has often sought to use federal funding as a cudgel to force Democratic and liberal jurisdictions into policy changes, especially in higher education, where the White House has threatened to cut off billions of dollars in support to targeted university systems.

In court documents this month, the administration admitted that it canceled a block of roughly $7.5 billion in Biden-era clean energy funding "based solely" on the fact the money was flowing to projects in Democratic-led states.

The cuts were not based on "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor," the Department of Energy conceded as part of early negotiations in a federal lawsuit from University of California researchers.

Instead, the grants were included on a list of cancellations announced in October "based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state, i.e., whether the recipient's location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State."

The department added that with one exception, 284 terminated grants were slated to fund projects in Democratic-led states or states that voted for Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024. The roughly 340 grants that survived the chopping block were "in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election" or had at least one Republican senator, according to court filings.
news.author: Josh Marcus

news.title: America is clear: It doesn’t like older lawmakers (but keeps voting for them anyway)
news.text:
Most Americans think lawmakers in Congress are just too old, according to a new poll, as Washington reels from the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, 71, and the lengthy hospitalization of Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84.

About 58 percent of Americans think the share of elderly lawmakers in Congress, which is currently one of the oldest in U.S. history, is a major problem, per a new CNN / SSRS poll.

That share rises to 68 percent for respondents younger than age 35.

Two-thirds of Americans, meanwhile, told the poll that elected officials should release all medical information about conditions that might impact their ability to serve. Just 25 percent thought politicians have the same right as regular citizens to keep their health records private.

And a whopping 70 percent of people aligned with the major parties said they would be uneasy or upset if the Republicans or Democrats nominated someone over age 70 for office.

The average age of Congress has been creeping up for decades, and the median age of current U.S. senators is 66, a disproportionately high age compared with the general population. 

Age concerns are back in the spotlight thanks to years of recent political turmoil.

In 2023, Sen. Dianne Feinstein died in office at age 90 while facing calls to step down amid questions about her declining memory and numerous health complications.

The following year, concerns about President Joe Biden’s health and mental fitness tanked his reelection campaign and led to Kamala Harris replacing him on the ballot. 

The trend has cut across parties and administrations.

President Trump has faced persistent questions about his own health and fitness, given that he regularly appears to fall asleep at public events and often is seen with bandages and makeup for a persistent medical condition on his hand.

In the Senate, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky has been absent from congressional business for more than 40 days after a fall in his home in June left him unconscious.

The senator has insisted he’s on the road to recovery, and has shared multiple photos and written statements updating the public about his condition.

Critics have argued the senator needs to do more to assure the public he can still serve.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, has demanded in a letter to the senator on Monday that he “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.” 

“If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve, I will insist Leader Thune fully investigate your condition, report to the American people, and begin the process if warranted,” Beshear added.

The Kentucky governor has also challenged CNN to call McConnell live on air, given claims from CNN contributor Scott Jennings that he recently spoke on the phone with McConnell. 

Age concerns have inspired calls for term limits and a more transparent process for evaluating and disclosing the health of lawmakers and candidates.

“The U.S. political system has virtually no objective standards to ensure that the people entrusted with the highest offices in the country remain physically and cognitively capable of performing some of the most important and demanding jobs in the world,” Anahita Dua, a vascular surgeon, wrote in a recent MS Now opinion piece. “That is no longer acceptable.”
news.summary: The recent death of Sen. Lindsey Graham and hospitalization of Sen. Mitch McConnell has reignited debate over whether lawmakers are too old to serve
news.author: Josh Marcus

news.title: Jim Clyburn is pointing the finger at all the wrong people
news.text:
In a recent podcast interview, Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., blamed Black voters in part for Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss in the 2024 presidential election. Clyburn typified a retrograde assumption many in the Democratic establishment hold: that certain voters ought to serve the party rather than the other way around. With the midterm elections looming and the start of a high-stakes presidential primary season around the corner, hearing such a dismissive view of voters expressed by a Democrat of Clyburn’s influence is particularly alarming.

Clyburn made that comment during a conversation with Vox’s Astead Herndon, who pressed the 86-year-old, 17-term representative to assign blame for the Democratic Party’s low approval ratings, including with its own voters. Clyburn, a former chair of the Congressional Black Caucus and a former House majority whip, blamed everyone but party leadership. The conversation got especially pointed when he and Herndon discussed Harris’ 2024 loss and Herndon asked Clyburn if he thought there was a political lesson to take from an administration whose central goal was to stop Donald Trump’s return to the White House. Clyburn answered: “When the white vote turned out 71% two years ago, and the Black vote turned out 59%, you tell me whose fault that is.” He later added that if that “59% had been 69%, she would have won.” When Herndon followed by asking if Clyburn was saying “Black people let Kamala Harris down,” he responded, “In many instances, absolutely.” 

Clyburn’s answer was an astonishing deflection.

Parties are not owed votes; they earn them. And racial minorities and marginalized communities — whether they are Black, women or Latino — shouldn’t be taken for granted as a lock for the Democratic Party just because it’s the party that embraces multiculturalism.

Politicians are supposed to be public servants.

Clyburn’s statement is sadly emblematic of establishment Democrats’ tendency to see ethnic minority voters only as people who vote as monolithic blocs. But they don’t. Just like white voters, they have interests across many policy areas — the economy, immigration, taxes, foreign policy and so on. And just like white voters, they can change their mind, be ambivalent about candidates and think in terms of strategic trade-offs. In the 2024 election, voters across all kinds of demographics were dissatisfied with the economy in the wake of a surge in inflation. The Democratic Party didn’t take their concerns seriously enough, and a candidate deploying Hitlerian rhetoric made gains with Latinos, Black men and Asian Americans compared with his first victory. 

There is some historical context that distinguishes Clyburn’s perspective from those of other members of party leadership. He grew up in the segregated South, where the battle for voting rights was won and where, after the Voting Rights Act became law, many Black people saw voting as a sacred duty. Black political power was and is deeply intertwined with participation in Democratic politics. But taking that vote for granted is antidemocratic, and can even be exploitative — and it does not obviate the need to listen to a community’s needs and perceptions. “Is there no reason that Black voters could not have felt heard” by the Democrats, Herndon asked Clyburn. “There might be. I’d like to know what it is,” Clyburn responded, seemingly implying that he couldn’t conceive of a good one or that no such reasonable views are out there.

Politicians are supposed to be public servants, and parties succeed in politics when they recognize the old adage about effective customer service: The customer is always right. (Or least needs to be understood and attended to in some fashion.) Sensitivity to what voters want in real time — rather than banking on the lesser-evil ballot or some fixed notion of what’s best for voters even when they say otherwise — is what helps parties build trust, identify sources of excitement and drive up voter turnout. That’s how you push that number up from 59%.

Clyburn’s blinkered worldview is consequential. He has been in Congress for more than three decades and served as House majority whip multiple times. His capacity as a power broker helped Joe Biden win the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020. Yet in that Vox interview, he strongly rejected the idea that Democratic leaders should engage in any big-picture introspection about what the party stands for. At various points, he blamed “media branding” for its beleaguered reputation. He said progressive challengers knocking out Democratic incumbents in the primaries does not signal a problem with the party but was the fault of individual low-performing candidates. Herndon interviewed Clyburn on his 86th birthday, and not surprisingly, Clyburn rejected the idea that the advanced age of many in the party is cause for concern. 

In what may be the most tragicomic example of being out of touch, Clyburn admitted that he hadn’t heard of ChatGPT until the week before the interview. No concern there. ChatGPT only symbolizes the way huge swaths of the workforce may eventually face job market apocalypse. Why should a politician of such influence know anything about the buzziest economic issue of recent years? 

Remarkably, Clyburn’s influence within the Democratic Party is still growing — with South Carolina jumping to the start of the Democratic presidential primary schedule, his role as kingmaker is larger than ever. But like so many Democrats of his generation, his ability to understand and influence the world itself is waning.
news.author: Ja’han Jones

news.title: Ruby Rippey breaks cover after salacious essay exposed Gavin Newsom affair details
news.text:
Ruby Rippey, the former lover of Gov. Gavin Newsom who reignited one of California’s biggest political scandals with a bombshell Vanity Fair essay Tuesday, was spotted walking her dog just hours after the story went viral.

Dressed casually, Rippey appeared carefree and relaxed as she enjoyed a sunny afternoon near her Marin County home following publication of the essay, which thrust her decades-old affair with Newsom back into the national spotlight.

Rippey served as an aide to Newsom when he was mayor of San Francisco and was married at the time to his campaign manager and close friend, Alex Tourk.

In the essay, Rippey accuses Newsom of sanitizing one of the defining scandals of his political career, arguing the governor reshaped key details of their affair in his memoir, “Young Man in a Hurry,” which was released as the governor is widely expected to mount a 2028 presidential campaign.

Newsom described the relationship as “the stupidest and also briefest of affairs,” writing that Rippey “was among a group of staffers who came to my apartment for a party. She was the last to leave.”

But Rippey said reading the memoir left her with “a familiar feeling … of being written about by someone who assumes I won’t answer.”

“He describes it as ‘the briefest of affairs.’ His sister, he notes, observed that I was ‘hanging a bit too close,'” Rippey wrote.

Instead, the affair appears to have lasted for some time and sexual encounters occurred in multiple places and overnight stays.

She also disputed Newsom’s account of how her husband learned about the affair, challenging his suggestion that he was the one who came clean to Tourk.

“That detail — subtle but significant — is the one that stays with me,” Rippey wrote. “It reads — to me, at least — as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done. Technically defensible, perhaps, but one that leaves the unmistakable impression that he, not I, was the one who told Alex the truth.”

Newsom’s office declined comment on the essay.

The affair remains one of the biggest stains of Newsom’s life and political career. Tourk resigned after confronting the mayor, who later held a news conference calling the affair a “personal lapse of judgment.”

“I want to make it clear that everything you’ve heard and read is true, and I am deeply sorry about that,” Newsom said at the time.

Rippey’s essay also renewed scrutiny of comments made by Jennifer Siebel Newsom, who was dating the future governor when the affair became public and publicly placed much of the blame on Rippey.

“I shouldn’t say this, but … if people did research into the scandal … the woman is the culprit,” Siebel Newsom told the San Francisco Chronicle.

Siebel Newsom later doubled down in comments on the SFist blog despite describing herself as “a total woman’s woman.”

“I’m a total woman’s woman, girls girl … what’s your definition of affair? … It was a few nothing incidents when she showed up passed out outside of his door … she is bad news,” Siebel Newsom wrote.

She also defended Newsom, saying he was dealing with “crises — divorce, the loss of his mother, the pressures of being mayor, etc. and he was vulnerable and lonely.”

Siebel Newsom later apologized after the comments sparked backlash.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

Sam Singer, a spokesman for Rippey at the time, bashed Siebel Newsom for her comments.

“Ms. Siebel is an actress. I understand her need for publicity. However, her comments are unbecoming of an actress or a lady,” Singer said.

Rippey, who has since remarried and says she has remained sober for years, wrote that the affair began in 2005 while Newsom was separated from his then-wife, Kimberly Guilfoyle, and Rippey was married to Tourk. 

She acknowledged she willingly entered the relationship but said she now recognizes the power imbalance between a mayor and one of his subordinates.

“Still, the [#MeToo] reckoning exposed what I had missed: Power does not need to coerce. It only needs to exist,” Rippey wrote. “The responsibility to hold the line belongs to the one who holds it. That didn’t happen. But I didn’t stumble into the space left open — I saw a possibility and went for it.”

She added, “Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly.”

Rippey also revealed that Kamala Harris, who at that time was San Francisco’s district attorney and still years away from becoming vice president, privately reached out after the scandal broke and urged her to stay silent.

“‘Just pause,” Harris told Rippey, according to the essay. “More time will give you better perspective.'”
news.summary: Ruby Rippey, the former lover of Gov. Gavin Newsom who reignited one of California's biggest political scandals with a bombshell Vanity Fair essay Tuesday, was spotted walking her dog just hours after the story went viral.

news.title: Special Congressional Election in Georgia Heads to Runoff
news.text:
Democrats Everton Blair and Marcye Scott are headed to a runoff in the special election in Georgia’s 13th Congressional District that was held on July 28.

Eliminated in the primary were Democrat Carlos Moore and Republicans Caesar Gonzales and Fayth Park.

Given that both runoff candidates are Democrats, whoever wins the Aug. 25 general election will narrow the Republican majority in the House of Representatives. That person will serve the remainder of Rep. David Scott’s (D-Ga.) term. David Scott died in April at the age of 80. Marcye Scott is David Scott’s daughter.

Blair, an educator, is the only candidate running in the special election who also ran in May for the congressional term beginning in January 2027.

In the primary, he finished third after earning roughly 12 percent of the vote.

news.title: Why Mark Ruffalo is missing from Spider-Man: Brand New Day's press tour: Spoiler fears, Palestine support, or a busy schedule?
news.text: While Tom Holland and Zendaya are doing the media rounds like the pros they are, one massive name has been conspicuously absent from the Spider-Man: Brand New Day press tour. Mark Ruffalo, who is set to appear as Bruce Banner/The Hulk in the upcoming blockbuster, is nowhere to be found. No talk show appearances, red carpets, or carefully worded interviews where he almost spills the beans. It's almost as if Marvel has placed a permanent mute button on the man. But given his track record, can you really blame them?When it comes to the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Mark Ruffalo is basically the cast member who you hand a sock to and tell him to sit in the corner. In 2017, the 58-year-old casually dropped that in the next movie, "everybody dies" on Good Morning America.This was, of course, a major spoiler for Avengers: Infinity War. Poor Don Cheadle was sitting right next to him, looking like he wanted to phase through the floor. And it wasn't a one-off mistake. Ruffalo previously accidentally live-streamed the audio of the Thor: Ragnarok premiere on Instagram for 10 minutes before realising. He would basically have been a PR nightmare wrapped in green spandex for director Destin Daniel Cretton.Pairing Mark Ruffalo and Tom Holland for promotional interviews is like leaving two toddlers unattended in a room full of explosives. Marvel learned their lesson the hard way. Benedict Cumberbatch, who had the unenviable task of sharing the press tour with Holland, once described feeling like his "babysitter," claiming it was like "avoiding grenades coming from the right and left". Can you imagine what would happen if Marvel unleashed both Ruffalo and Holland on the same interviewer? It would be chaos.While his spoiler habit is legendary, Ruffalo's absence is also being connected to his outspoken politics. A staunch critic of Donald Trump and his policies, he has been a vocal supporter of Palestine, recently backing the historical film Palestine 36 through a series of special screenings and conversations.The film, which explores the Arab revolt against British colonial rule in 1936, is described as "one of the greatest and most important films" about the history of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Ruffalo's known for his leftist views, even helping organise an Avengers-themed video to support Kamala Harris. In the current political climate, Disney might have thought it wise to keep their star away from any potential on-camera eruptions. Believers of this theory believe this could have been Rachel Zegler's Snow White promotion had Ruffalo been involved.There is a more boring but practical explanation for Ruffalo's absence from the Spider-Man press tour. According to reports, Ruffalo is currently busy shooting the second season of the HBO crime drama Task. The show began production in Philadelphia earlier this month, making it logistically difficult for him to join the promotional circuit. However, Marvel has a history of hiding their actors from the press due to their track record, so the "busy schedule" excuse might just be a convenient cover for "we can't trust him anywhere near a microphone."Fans have taken to social media with their theories, and they're not holding back. One user on X hilariously pointed out, "Marvel learned their lesson after Infinity War.... Mark Ruffalo giving promotional interviews for Spider-Man: Brand New Day would just mean the entire plot gets spoiled in 5 minutes flat. Marvel keeping him away from mics is top-tier strategy." Another simply said, "Probably cos Marvel would snipe him for accidentally spoiling smth again."Some have highlighted his political views as the real reason. One commenter said, "Because he runs his mouth about the president too much and marvel seems like they want a home run hit." Another harshly added, "Excellent, we don't want to hear is crazy leftist views when thinking about the Hulk."Whether it's due to his history of spoiling movies, his political firebrand status, or just a simple scheduling conflict, keeping Mark Ruffalo away from the Spider-Man microphones might just be the smartest PR decision Marvel has made in years. The guy is a fantastic actor, but when it comes to keeping secrets, he makes the Hulk look like a master of subtlety.Spider-Man: Brand New Day releases in theatres on July 31. In India, the movie has an early release, coming to theatres on July 30.

news.title: Kamala Harris 'Told Gavin Newsom's Former Mistress to Pause and Not Make a Public Comment' About Their Steamy Affair
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris has been dragged into California Governor Gavin Newsom's latest scandal.

The woman who had an affair with Newsom, Ruby Rippey, claimed Harris encouraged her to stay silent about the affair back in 2005. With that feedback in mind, Rippey, who was an aide under Newsom at the time, remained quiet until now, RadarOnline.com has learned.Kamala Harris Offers Ruby Rippey AdviceAt the time, Newsom was the mayor of San Francisco. When the press heard news of an affair in his office, Newsom's girlfriend at the time publicly played down the fling, chalking it up to "a few nothing incidents." 

Rippey was publicly branded "bad news."

She was offered opportunities to speak, according to her explosive essay in Vanity Fair, including a potential memoir offer. However, Harris, who was the district attorney at the time, gave her a phone call.

Rippey recalled Harris, whom she called "a real girl's girl," allegedly telling her, "I wouldn’t say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective."

Harris' guidance was "the best advice I received," confessed Rippey. She reflected, realizing at the time she was still fresh into the emotional turbulence, "unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it." 

Rippey resolved, "So I stayed silent."Rippey Opens Up About California ScandalThe affair, which first went public in 2007, lasted intermittently from 2005 to 2006. Rippey was married at the time to Newsom's campaign manager Alex Tourk. Newsom, while separated from then-wife Kimberly Guilfoyle, was still legally married, with the divorce not yet finalized.

While the relationship didn't officially begin until 2005, Rippey claimed she felt the weight of Newsom's desire starting in 2004. She claimed in her essay he noticed him "looking at me." 

Plus, she recalled the 58-year-old telling her, "You look really good." Rippey leaned into the desire, becoming more intentional with the clothes she wore to the office.Gavin Newsom and Rippey's Affair Begins in 2005In July 2005, Rippey recalled attending a wedding in Napa Valley. When the night turned to partying, her husband chose to leave while Rippey went back to an inn with Newsom.

She wrote, "I wake the next morning beside him, still dressed. I am cold, almost shivering, and my dress – the one my mother warned me not to wear – is soaked from the waist down. I had passed out."

"The boundaries begin to disintegrate," she claimed. It wasn't necessarily discreet, as Rippey claimed others in the office began to notice.

Nonetheless, they continued to meet periodically. She penned, "We meet, and we drink. There is s--, but it isn’t the point. The point is proximity – to power, to being chosen, to feeling newly visible."

For Rippey, "it feels like oxygen."Rippey Accuses Newsom of Inaccuracies in MemoirUltimately, Rippey resigned from her post in 2006 after battling with drugs and alcohol. She decided to get sober, which she did not believe would be possible in her professional position nor while staying in the affair. 

She maintained the affair was not what caused her downward spiral, but rather it "just gave it somewhere to live."

In 2007, Rippey penned an email to her husband with the confession before returning home from rehab. When she returned home, Tourk was "measured" in his response. When Tourk eventually confronted Newsom, Rippey claimed, "there is no straight answer" about the affair. 

Tourk's resignation sparked the media hysteria which would ultimately lead to Rippey's call with Harris. Newsom owned up to the affair. 

"Everything you've heard and read is true," he claimed. 

Rippey was later inspired to come forward after Newsom penned his own memoir. 

In the pages of the text, according to Rippey, Newsom downplayed their relationship. 

Plus, she alleged, Newsom falsely claimed he was the one who eventually confessed to Tourk.

news.title: Trump’s ‘embarrassing’ comment about LeBron has ESPN host speaking up: ‘Beyond the pale"
news.text:
It’s no secret that ESPN host Stephen A. Smith and NBA star LeBron James don’t get along.

On Monday, Smith defended James after President Donald Trump called James “racist” last week when taking questions from reporters.

This, even for a hot take machine like Smith, was “beyond the pale.”

“It’s embarrassing,” Smith said in a video posted on YouTube. “You’re the commander-in-chief, you’re the president of the United States, and you’re going to come out and you’re going to call this black man, who’s universally recognized one of the greatest athletes who have ever lived, who has been an upstanding citizen, somebody I don’t get along with, and I’m still willing to concede he’s great.”

Smith argued that Trump is resorting to calling James racist simply because James has never supported Trump politically.

James endorsed Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and Kamala Harris in 2024. 

“The only Democratic candidate LeBron James ever really stood up for was Barack Obama,” Smith said. “Everything since then has basically been anti-Trump over the last three elections.”

Last week, Trump claimed new Philadelphia 76ers superstar might be “a racist” after weighing in on the debate over who is the greatest basketball player of all time.

When Trump responded to the question from Fox News’ Peter Doocy on Friday, the president pointed to his personal relationship and not statistics to settle the debate between James and Chicago Bulls legend Michael Jordan.

“Well, Michael Jordan’s a guy that’s a friend of mine — play golf with him. He’s a really good guy. And I think LeBron is — maybe he’s a racist. But maybe he doesn’t like Trump, I don’t know. But I only like people that like me. So I would say Michael Jordan all the way,” Trump said.

news.title: GOP Congressman Claims His Opponent Is Under FBI Investigation, But Can’t Prove It
news.text:
WASHINGTON ― Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) has represented a Democratic-leaning district north of Philadelphia since 2017, repeatedly winning reelection with a combination of a nice guy persona and a bipartisan voting record. 

As he takes on yet another Democratic challenger in the roughest political environment for Republicans in years, Fitzpatrick is heavily pushing a nasty and unproven accusation about his opponent. 

In TV ads, mailers and billboards, Fitzpatrick has said his opponent Bob Harvie, a member of the Bucks County Board of Commissioners, is “under FBI investigation” for corruption. 

There’s not much evidence for the accusation. Harvie did speak to a grand jury in 2022 as part of an investigation into local governments in suburban Philadelphia, though no indictments resulted and the exact targets of the investigation have never been reported. How does Fitzpatrick know the case is still ongoing? 

“I am a former FBI agent, but I know how grand juries work, and I’m well aware of his status in this case,” Fitzpatrick, who worked as a federal prosecutor and FBI agent before running for office in 2017, told HuffPost. “I’m aware of what’s contained in the files that he refuses to release.”

Harvie has furiously denied the accusation and sent a cease-and-desist letter to Fitzpatrick’s campaign, to no avail. 

“He’s desperate to hold on to the seat,” Harvie told HuffPost. “He sees the same polling that I see ― that he’s in trouble, that his party’s in trouble, that Donald Trump is an albatross around the neck of Republicans, and that the policies they put in place are hurting people up and down this county, this district, and that’s why he’s throwing these lies out about me because he doesn’t have anything else to talk about.”

The stakes are high: Fitzpatrick is one of only three Republicans currently representing a district that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, and Democrats view the seat as an important pickup opportunity in their quest to retake the House this fall. 

Fitzpatrick has broken with his party on all manner of topics, from the war in Iran to gun control to taxes and the social safety net. He voted against final passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill last year, the legislation that slashed food benefits and Medicaid to pay for tax cuts tilted toward the wealthy. But the Fitzpatrick-Harvie showdown so far seems to be mostly about Fitzpatrick’s claim that Harvie is being looked at by the FBI. 

There is no official public information to corroborate or refute the claim that Harvie is under an FBI investigation. The FBI declined to comment.

Harvie has said he testified to the grand jury only as a witness. Fitzpatrick acknowledges Harvie wasn’t the target of the investigation, but insists he’s an investigative subject rather than a mere witness, meaning his conduct is at issue. 

Harvie’s attorney strenuously disagrees: “Harvie is not now and has never been the subject of any criminal investigation,” they wrote in the cease-and-desist letter to Fitzpatrick’s campaign.

“You know what would solve this whole mystery? It’s not a mystery for me, but for you all ― have him release his file,” Fitzpatrick said. He’s also said that if Harvie’s so sure he’s lying, all he has to do is file the lawsuit he’s threatening in his cease-and-desist letter, though the legal process could take weeks, if not months, and not resolve before the election. 

Harvie said there’s no file for him to release, that he doesn’t have any paperwork related to the case. He made some not-so-nice comments of his own about Fitzpatrick.

“He has a $5 million house in California. He’s got a $2 million house in D.C. He’s got another house here in Bucks County that I’m not even sure he lives in,” Harvie said. “He’s obviously now married to a Fox News reporter who’s considerably younger than he is, and so I just think he’s got a lifestyle he likes now, and he’s desperate, you know, and really he’s forgotten about the people of this district.”

news.title: WATCH: Battleground Democrat called Iowa a 'backwater' over transgender athletes ban
news.text: A Democrat hoping to flip one of the country’s most competitive House seats called her state a "backwater" over Republican efforts to bar transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports, according to unearthed footage obtained by Fox News Digital. House candidate Christina Bohannan made the comments during a 2021 legislative forum while opposing a GOP proposal barring biological males from competing on female sports teams. Bohannan's comments could provide fresh ammunition for Republicans as the repeat candidate seeks a third bid against Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, in a swing district that President Donald Trump carried by more than eight points in 2024. "They’re introducing these bills and making these comments to try to make a point," Bohannan, who previously served in the Iowa state legislature, said, referring to her GOP colleagues. "And I think even that is really damaging to people and sends a very bad message about our state that’s going to make the state look like a backwater." FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME Iowa, under Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, enacted a transgender athletes ban in 2022. Bohannan voted against the measure. The comments are the latest instance of Bohannan torching Iowa for rejecting left-wing policies. Bohannan also said in 2021 the Hawkeye State would be seen as "backwards" if lawmakers approved a bill prohibiting diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) training at public schools and universities. Reynolds signed the legislation later that year. "I think that it's going to send a very bad message about Iowa and that it is going to seem like…this backwards state that doesn't understand there are things like systemic racism," the Democrat hopeful said on the "Under the Dome" podcast in 2021. Bohannan notably served as chairwoman of the University of Iowa College of Law's DEI committee, where she urged students to support the Black Lives Matter movement, Fox News Digital previously reported. In that role, she sent students a letter encouraging them to financially contribute to several activist funds, some of which supported defunding police. Bohannan lost to Miller-Meeks by fewer than 800 votes in 2024, making it the closest House race in the nation. She also launched a failed run for the seat in 2022. BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT FLIP-FLOPS ON CONVERSION THERAPY AFTER LEFT-WING BACKLASH The nonpartisan Cook Political Report says the rematch contest is a "toss-up." The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), which is aggressively working to re-elect Miller-Meeks to a third House term, sharply criticized Bohannan's remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Liberal Christina Bohannan didn't just vote against protecting girls' sports, she mocked Iowans for standing up for women and girls," NRCC spokeswoman Emily Tuttle said. "Bohannan has made it clear she's for they/them, not Iowa families," Tuttle continued, invoking Trump's signature attack line against former Vice President Kamala Harris. Fox News Digital reached out to Bohannan for comment. Bohannan's remarks come as transgender issues continue to split Democrats, while public polling has shown broad support for limiting girls' and women's sports to biological females. A New York Times/Ipsos poll released in 2025 found that nearly eight in 10 Americans opposed biological males participating in women’s sports. Roughly 70% of Democrats or Democrat-leaning respondents held the same position, according to the survey. Miller-Meeks cheered the Supreme Court in June upholding state-level bans on biological males participating on female sports teams. "I have and will continue to fight to ensure every female athlete has a fair chance." Bohannan, by contrast, did not appear to publicly comment on the ruling. news.title: Why Access Is the Real Back-To-School Challenge for Black Students
news.text:
“You’re here because you belong here. Now channel the confidence of a mediocre White man.”

I whispered those words to an HBCU journalism student whose hands were shaking as she looked up to address Vice President Kamala Harris and Keisha Lance Bottoms in the White House’s mock briefing room. Moments later, her nerves gave way to sharp, well-researched questions. Watching her and her fellow HBCU students rise to the occasion confirmed what I’ve long believed: talent has never been the problem. Access is.

During my time as White House director of African American media, one of the initiatives I was proudest to create brought HBCU journalism students into the White House to interview senior administration officials. 

The goal was never to give them a tour. It was to give them access.

Because once you ask a question of the first Black vice president of the United States or sit where history is reported every day, you begin to see yourself as the professional you’re training to be. You’re not only building your resume but the confidence to command any room you step foot in.

Throughout my career on Capitol Hill and the White House, I met brilliant young people with endless potential. What they lacked was someone willing to open a door.

Those advantages have often been passed through family connections, alumni networks, and professional circles. If you weren’t born into those networks, you often missed out on information that others inherited.

It was never a coincidence when a colleague’s last name was the same as a well-known Democratic donor or a friend of the President himself.

My colleagues and I would joke about the “nepo babies,” but it wasn’t a laughing matter because these were the people who had access to information, networks, and influential relatives willing to explain the unwritten rules of a game we’d never been invited to play.

As students prepare to head back to campus, they’re often told to earn good grades, join organizations, and build a résumé.

All of that matters.

But students can’t pursue opportunities they don’t know exist. They can’t build relationships with people they’ve never met. They can’t imagine themselves in rooms when they can’t find the door.

Today’s students are entering a workforce that is more competitive than ever. Entry-level jobs are harder to secure. Many organizations have scaled back programs designed to broaden access to careers in fields like government, media, and business.

That makes individual action even more important. Most of us can’t invite students to the White House but every one of us has a door we can open. We can share the lessons we learned the hard way.

That’s why I created The Loewe Key Initiative to connect Black students and recent graduates with the knowledge, relationships, and entry-level opportunities that they may not even know are possible. Through mentorship, career conversations, networking, internships, and practical advice, I hope to help talented young Black people spend less time trying to find the door and more time preparing themselves to walk through it.

As another school year begins, more of us should ask ourselves one simple question:

Who opened the first door for me? Then let’s honor them by opening one for someone else.

Erica Loewe is a former Biden-Harris White House official and founder of the Loewe Key Initiative for Black Students and Recent Graduates.
news.summary:
A former White House official breaks down why closing the information gap is critical for Black students—because no one can pursue opportunities they don’t know exist.

news.text:
For many voters, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires marked an end to their support for Mayor Karen Bass. In their dissent, Angelenos routinely point to property damage, air pollution, school cancellations, and other events that could have been at least partially prevented.

However, the label of “Democratic Socialist” that her opponent, Nithya Raman, carries may escort the incumbent candidate into the proverbial winner’s circle this November.
Prediction market
traders currently have Karen Bass listed at 63¢ per contract to defeat Raman in the general election.

Why Karen Bass?

More than $120 million has already been traded on Kalshi’s Los Angeles mayoral race winner market. Although Bass is currently 72 years old, she is a veteran of the public service sector. Bass served as a member of the US House of Representatives for over ten years before becoming mayor of Los Angeles. She also served as the speaker of the California State Assembly from 2008 to 2010.

Karen Bass has the endorsements of former vice president Kamala Harris and former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi. By contrast, Nithya Raman has only been in public service since 2020, as a councilmember representing the city’s 4th District.

Although polling shows that the majority of Los Angeles voters believe the city is on the “wrong track,” they’re expected to balk this November when faced with a clear “yes/no” vote between Bass and Raman. The Democratic Socialist Raman’s proposed policies may be viewed as

of a shift from how liberals have traditionally ruled the nation’s second-largest city. This is why we’re choosing Bass at 63 cents per contract to win the general election.

What could catapult Nithya Raman?

Born in 1981, Nithya Raman has a decisive age advantage over the incumbent. Her progressive politics resonate with a growing number of Angelenos and her experience as an advocate for individuals who are homeless adds to those progressive credentials.

Raman’s base, renters who reside in Los Feliz and Silver Lake, have taken an immediate liking to rent-control policies that have made their way to New York and would likely be possible if the mayoral race is decided in Raman’s favor. As an immigrant herself, Nithya Raman is in a far better political position to push back on enforcement practices that the federal government has engaged in, especially since some of those controversial enforcement actions have taken place in Los Angeles.

If Nithya Raman can retain her core base while making at least some appeal to more moderate voters, she may overcome the polling and prediction market advantage that Karen Bass has enjoyed throughout the race.

Spencer Pratt has been eliminated from contention

Spencer Pratt was denied an opportunity to compete directly against Karen Bass earlier this year when he placed third in the Primary Nominating Election. November’s general election for Los Angeles mayor will basically be a “run-off” between the two candidates who received the most votes on June 2nd.

In the end, we don’t believe Karen Bass will be defeated on November 3rd. Look for the experienced public servant to remain in office as Los Angeles mayor through the 2030 calendar year.

news.title: Maine Dem in hot seat for championing popular vote despite clinching Senate bid without it
news.text: Despite past calls to make the popular vote the deciding factor for presidential elections in Maine, Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine, is facing backlash for embracing his newfound Democratic Party nomination despite a process that circumvented the usual statewide consideration. The Maine Senate election spun out of control for Democrats earlier this month when sexual assault allegations emerged against the party’s official candidate, Graham Platner. Scrambling in response to the fallout, Maine Democrats announced they would create an open process, allowing potential replacement candidates to submit their intent to run and begin collecting signatures to appear on the ballot. Then, a convention of 601 delegates would vote to select the new nominee. FORMER PLATNER ALLY TROY JACKSON LOCKS DOWN DELEGATES AS TOP RIVALS FOR DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOMINATION DROP OUT "We have worked hard to create a fair process that is inclusive of varying viewpoints and diverse backgrounds of Democrats across the state of Maine, as we all come together in service of our ultimate goal: defeat Susan Collins and win this Senate seat," the Maine Democrats website states. "These circumstances are unprecedented, but our state party is ready and capable of rising to this challenge." Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, unleashed on Jackson and the process that made him the nominee. "It’s become increasingly clear that Troy Jackson will shapeshift into anything he needs to in order to gain power – including abandoning the belief that voters should decide elections," Cianci said in a statement. "Mainers want a senator they can trust, not a snake-oil-salesman standing ready to sell them out at a moment’s notice," she added. But even before the process began, political observers believed Jackson, a fellow progressive like Platner, would prevail. Like Platner, Jackson has called for universal healthcare, the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), severing U.S. military aid to Israel and raising taxes on the nation’s top earners. TOP DEM HOPEFUL FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER YEARS IN SOCIALIST ORBIT WITH PUZZLING CLAIM Shannon Watts, a political activist and commentator who opposed Platner’s nomination, wasted no time in blasting Jackson as a possible alternative. "So no, we’re not going to pick this f---ing guy," Watts said, anticipating the party’s progressive support for Jackson despite his own reported misconduct. Jackson allegedly threw a water bottle at fellow Democratic state senator Heather Sanborn in 2021, an outburst Jackson has since apologized for. Despite apprehension from Watts and concern from other Democrats about pre-selecting a candidate, of the 601 delegates at the Maine convention on Saturday, 456 came out already committed to Jackson’s nomination — roughly 75% of the delegates. In the end, Jackson won 566 delegates, or 94% of the total support. Jackson did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether he saw his nomination as a circumvention of the regular primary process. In the past, Jackson has stressed the importance of Democratic participation. "I've always believed that our democracy is at its best when everyone has a chance to participate – whether I agree with you on an issue or not," Jackson posted on X in 2020 leading up to a Maine Democratic primary. In 2019, he sponsored legislation that would have Maine award its electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, citing his support for direct democracy. "Let’s total all the votes up across the country, and whoever gets the most votes wins; that seems a simple premise to me," Jackson told local media outlets in 2019. Since his nomination, Jackson has insisted he can represent all factions of the Democratic Party, even without a statewide vote to cement his nomination. "There is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement. And I will spend every day now through November earning that trust, because today we turn the page. Today, this becomes a general election campaign, and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November," Jackson said after his nomination. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT IF PLATNER DROPS OUT? HERE'S WHO COULD REPLACE HIM ON THE BALLOT AND HOW IT WOULD WORK CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Notably, Jackson has attracted the endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris — another Democratic figure who stepped in at the 11th hour to rescue a campaign. "I know what it is like to step up to the plate with a short runway to Election Day. Troy will have just 101 days between his nomination for Senate and when voters in Maine will cast their ballots," Harris said in a fundraising email on Monday.
news.summary: Troy Jackson secured 75% of delegate votes at Maine's convention, but critics say the process contradicts his own calls for popular vote democracy.

news.title: The View’s Number of Conservative Guests Swells to 5, Compared to 87 Liberals
news.text:
Season 29 of ABC’s The View came ended last week amid an ongoing battle with the Federal Communications Commission over their purported status as a “bona fide news program,” which called into question their bias, their content, and their adherence to the so-called equal time rule for political candidates. Compared to a previous long-term study of The View’s guests, a new NewsBusters study discovered the number of guests to express a conservative political opinion more than doubled… to five, compared to the 87 guests to express a liberal one.

"The View’s 87-5 guest ratio proves the show is not diverse at all. It’s a Democrat Socialist Party infomercial," Media Research Center President David Bozell said.

For the entire run of Season 29 (September 8, 2025 - July 24, 2026) The View interviewed a total of 321 guests.

Of the 87 liberal guests, 16 of them were Democratic politicians: former Senator Joe Manchin (WV), former Vice President Kamala Harris, two appearances by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani before and after he was elected, former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, Senator Bernie Sanders (VT), Senator John Fetterman (PA), Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett (TX), Congressman Jim Clyburn (SC), Governor Josh Shapiro (PA), Texas State House Member James Talarico, Governor Andy Beshear (KY), Senator Cory Booker (NJ), former politician Rahm Emanuel (IL), Senator Chris Murphy (CT), and former First Lady Jill Biden.

The View also welcomed two of the liberal Supreme Court Justices, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, as well as former White House Press Secretary Karine Jean-Pierre.

The show was also a gathering place for the liberal media elite: Jon Karl (ABC), Scott Galloway, Abby Phillip (CNN), Stephen A. Smith (ESPN), Ken Burns, Don Lemon, Martha Raddatz (ABC), Maggie Haberman (NYT), and Jonathan Swan (New York Times).

Liberal comedians got a lot of love too: Hasan Minhaj (twice), Leslie Jones, Sarah Sherman, Matt Friend, Amber Ruffin, Taylor Tomlinson, Chelsea Handler, Ismael Loutfi, Kathy Griffin, and Wanda Sykes, to name a few.

The left-wing of the Hollywood crowd was also well represented, here’s some of the more prominent names: America Ferrera, Henry Winkler, Ethan Hawke, Jamie Lee Curtis, Noah Schnapp, Morgan Freeman, Nathan Lane, Stephen Lang, LeVar Burton, Sigourney Weaver, RuPaul, and Molly Ringwald.

Then there were the five conservative / right-leaning guests: Actress Cheryl Hines, former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene (GA), Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, Trump attorney Alina Habba, and Vice President J.D. Vance.

As NewsBusters noted in our 2025 guest examination (which included the latter half of Season 28 and the first half of Season 29), the first two right-leaners come with asterisks next to their names. 

The first one wasn’t invited on until over a month into Season 29: actress Cheryl Hines. Despite being there to hawk her own book, Hines was married to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and having her on was a way for them to beat up on him via proxy. While having left-wing politics herself, she was forced to defend her husband’s - and by extension the Trump administration’s - policies, thus she was counted as right-leaning.

The second conservative, was former Georgia Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, who was the first GOP politician who was then-currently in office The View had hosted since New Hampshire Governor Chris Sununu was on in August 2024. As NewsBusters reported at the time, they only had Greene on because she was being a headache for Congressional Republican leadership during the government shutdown. The cast also tried to recruit her to become a Democrat.

Greene made a total of three appearances in Season 29 (the most of any individual), but she was only counted as a right-winger in one of them. In her first appearance, she stuck up for the Trump administration as the cast tried to get her to turn on him.

However, her second two appearances occurred after she had left office and was openly attacking Trump and Republicans in Congress. This meant she would be counted as a liberal since she was pushing their arguments against the right.

Not included in the guest count total were the guest co-hosts who filled in for “conservative” co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin while she was on maternity leave. They were excluded because they were on the show as co-hosts and not purely as guests.

For the sake of completion, those women were Elisabeth Hasselbeck, Sara Eisen, Savannah Chrisley, Amanda Carpenter, Abby Huntsman (who whiffed when asked about her conservative values), comedian Sheryl Underwood (who would later fill in for Joy Behar), and comedian Whitney Cummings (who called herself a “life long progressive” and suggested President Trump was sending child soldiers to fight Iran).

During the same show they grilled Hines, Behar claimed that Republicans wouldn’t go on the show because “they’re afraid of us.” This statement led to a slew of prominent conservative influencers, journalists (including NewsBusters), and politicians coming forward with evidence of the show either rejecting or ignoring their appearance requests (including people they had on previously).

The View cast responded on their podcast by suggesting most conservatives didn’t live up to the “certain caliber of guest” they felt the show demanded, that they only wanted to speak to the people they talked about on the show.

One of the notable conservatives they refused to have in Season 29 was The Daily Wire’s Isabel Brown, who they attacked and smeared because she had encouraged women to get married and have kids.

Brown reached out to The View to see if they would allow a conversation with her on their show. They rejected her request and lied to her about being booked up for weeks, while they continued to attack and smear her.

So much for wanting to speak with the people they talk about on the show. But The View had an answer to that too.

Farah Griffin basically admitted they didn’t want guests who would actually push back, call them out, and embarrass them.

ABC and The View did not respond to a request for comment.

Methodology: For a guest to be counted as either liberal or conservative, they needed to express such views during their appearance on The View. If a celebrity did not discuss politics, they were not included in the count of political leanings even if they had a history of being outspoken in the past. For example, actor Robert De Niro had a history of speaking out against President Trump, but was not included in the liberal count because politics did not come up.

Season 29 of ABC’s The View came ended last week amid an ongoing battle with the Federal Communications Commission over their purported status as a “bona fide news program,” which called into question their bias, their content, and their adherence to the so-called equal time rule for political candidates. news.title: US-Israel alliance pushed toward a bitter Democratic split over Gaza war and Netanyahu
news.text: For generations, support for Israel united Washington. Now Israel's attacks on Gaza, the Iran war and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close ties to US Republicans are eroding Democratic backing, threatening to turn one of America's closest alliances into a partisan divide.Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries, and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.The shift is evident in Congress. This month, nearly half of House Democrats voted for a failed amendment to cut off aid to Israel, legislation that once likely would have been defeated by an overwhelming bipartisan majority. Israel receives $3.8 billion annually in US military aid and received billions more in emergency funds in recent years.House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and some of his lieutenants opposed the measure, calling it overly broad. But former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark were among those voting yes.Democrats are increasingly divided over whether military aid should continue unchanged, be restricted to defensive weapons or be halted altogether.Vigorous debate and a hope for bipartisan restoration of supportUS Senator Chris Coons of Delaware, the leading Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he hopes Israeli elections in October help restore bipartisan US support while opening a new chapter beyond Netanyahu's leadership."New governments get to change direction," Coons told Reuters, adding, "Netanyahu has kept Israel at war for years now, partly to avoid the political consequences of his choices."Overall sentiment toward Israel is declining. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017."Yes, there is a vigorous debate, but across broad segments of the parties, support for Israel remains firmly in the mainstream," said Danny Danon, Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, in an interview. Israel a flashpoint in Michigan Democratic raceThe shift faces a major test in Tuesday's Democratic US Senate primary in Michigan, where voters will weigh competing visions of US support with growing numbers of congressional Democrats questioning longstanding US military aid.The race between progressive Abdul El-Sayed and US Representative Haley Stevens will determine who faces Republican Mike Rogers in November and reflects the wider Democratic debate over Israel and longstanding US military support.Stevens made a video with AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a major donor to her campaign, arguing that a close relationship with Israel "yields trade, that yields economic growth and that keeps our freedoms safe."By contrast, El-Sayed, a former public health official, told Fox News: "The question is whether we want a politics where our money is sent over to Israel to fund genocide and apartheid instead of investing in our own kids."A U.N. inquiry and several human rights groups have accused Israel of committing genocide in its military's devastation of Gaza, an allegation Israel rejects, saying it is fighting Hamas and taking steps to reduce civilian harm.Israeli policy has been a factor in other battleground congressional races, including New York, Florida and Colorado.Democratic support for Israel erodesStrains with Democrats deepened 11 years ago, when in a speech to Congress at the request of the Republican majority, Netanyahu attacked a deal crafted by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, on controlling Iran's nuclear program.Sentiment critical of Israel grew after Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack, in which nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals were killed and hundreds were taken hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed, according to Gaza health officials.Israel's bombardment of Gaza has reshaped Democratic politics, fueling a backlash among younger voters and deepening a generational divide within the party.Campus protests in 2024 intensified pressure on Democrats to reassess support for Israel. Some analysts say President Joe Biden's refusal to do so contributed to Democratic nominee Kamala Harris' loss to Trump later that year.Adding to tensions, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for Netanyahu's arrest for alleged war crimes.This primary election cycle, some establishment candidates have been defeated by more progressive challengers who have questioned support for Israel, mostly in congressional districts dominated by Democrats.Jeremy Ben-Ami, president of J Street, a progressive pro-Israel rival to AIPAC, said the debate within the Democratic Party reflected a backlash against the right-wing Netanyahu and AIPAC, calling it "a toxic brew that really has helped to make Israel, unfortunately, a real wedge issue in the Democratic Party."AIPAC did not respond to requests for comment.Shibley Telhami, a University of Maryland professor of government and politics and senior non-resident fellow at the Brookings Institution, called it a "paradigm shift that sees Israel now as a villain, even a genocidal villain, in a way that was never the case before."While some conservative influencers have joined the attack, the Republican Party will support Israel as long as evangelical Christians and Trump stand firm, Telhami said in an interview.Israel reshapes political battlegroundsThe divide over Israel is spilling into congressional campaigns elsewhere.Republican Representative Mike Lawler, who represents a district outside New York City with a large Jewish population, has used the Democratic shift on Israel to attack challenger Cait Conley in a battleground fight for control of the House.In southern Florida, moderate Representative Jared Moskowitz, a consistent supporter of Israel aid, is being challenged in the August 18 Democratic primary by democratic socialist Oliver Larkin, who campaigns on his belief that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza and supports an immediate suspension of US military aid to Israel.Recent opinion polls show Moskowitz leading Larkin by 32 percentage points.Longtime US Representative Diana DeGette was defeated in the Colorado Democratic primary by Ethiopian-born Melat Kiros. Kiros has called for ending wars, including by stopping military aid to Israel, while DeGette said she supported sending only defensive weapons to Israel.US Senator Mazie Hirono, who has advocated for a two-state solution and more humanitarian aid for Palestinians, said, "I think the support for Israel's right to exist, all of that is there. It's just the (Israeli) leadership we seriously question."
