news.title: Election Protection for the Midterms, Plus “The Odyssey” for Filmgoers
news.text:
Jon Wiener: From The Nation magazine, this is Start Making Sense. I’m Jon Wiener. Later in the hour: Elon Musk calls Christopher Nolan’s film “The Odyssey” “part of a left-wing plan” to “destroy Western Civilization.” John Powers has a different view – he’s critic-at-large on NPR’s “Fresh Air” with Terry Gross. But first: election protection – Skye Perriman will comment – in a minute.[BREAK]We have less than 100 days to the midterms, where Trump has various plans to undermine Democratic voting. To talk about election protection, we turn to Skye Perryman. She’s president and CEO of Democracy Forward, a leading election protection legal group. After starting out at Midway High School in Waco, Texas, now we read about her work in The New York Times and The Washington Post. We see her frequently on MSNBC and CNN. The news last week was that she had met with Chuck Schumer and other legal experts who were members of the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force. Skye Perryman, welcome to the program.

Skye Perryman: Great to be with you.

JW: Let’s start with that Senate task force. Who else is on it? What did you do at your meeting with Schumer last week?

SP: This is a task force that’s comprised of a range of members of the Senate, as well as election protection experts and lawyers and senior government officials, nonprofit and nonpartisan leaders, lawyers who have spent their careers defending the right to vote. People like Marc Elias are in the room to make sure that people in this country are going to be able to vote and that their votes are counted, because unlike in prior elections, right now, our federal government, our executive branch, our president and his allies are actively working to undermine the ability of people to vote.

JW: Trump, of course, has been working hard at attacking Democratic voting. And just to review his record here, he’s had only one really big victory. And that was when the Supreme Court justices he nominated eviscerated the Voting Rights Act, which led to the creation of more Republican House districts. But aside from that, Trump has been mostly failing, mostly losing. The courts have blocked his efforts to enlist the Postal Service in undermining voting by mail. That was an appeals court ruling just last Friday. The courts have also blocked his efforts to force states to hand over their voter rolls so that he can check them. He’s lost all 17 voter roll cases decided by district courts. No judge has ordered a state to provide an unredacted voter list to Trump and his people. And of course, he’s failed in his efforts to get the Senate to pass his SAVE Act, you know, restricting voting by imposing I.D. requirements. So, what do you think his next move will be after this string of losses? What are his next moves that are the most threatening for some of our friends? They think he’ll declare a national emergency as a basis for sending ICE agents, or maybe the military to blue polling places on Election Day to intimidate voters there under the pretext of preventing fraud. I imagine you and your group have thought about that one.

SP: We have. I mean, let me just start by saying you’re absolutely right that the administration continues to lose across the board, in the courts and even this US Supreme Court. You saw Amy Coney Barrett in a decision this last term being very clear that the United States Constitution does not provide a role for the president in our elections. So that’s the background on which all of this is happening. So, we believe he could try to do a variety of things. Many people are worried about a national emergency. The thing I will say about that is that the president would have to have a lawful basis for declaring one, and this is an administration that has made a range of announcements that have been blocked by the courts, because often they’re arbitrary. The president would have to carry out his plans through federal agencies. Those federal agencies are losing in court. They’re held accountable through our civil system. And so that’s not to – we don’t want everyone to be naive here or be particularly relaxed. But we do need to focus on people voting, making sure they’re registering to vote, making a plan to vote and understanding that the lawyers will be able to bring cases against these things. You mentioned the military, and I want to be very clear that federal law spells out and could not be more clear that the military cannot be engaged in and around polling places or in elections. There is an express federal law against that. There is an express federal law that criminalizes any federal officer that tries to intimidate people with respect to voting, which could become very which could become very relevant with respect to ICE. So, that is not to provide people cold comfort, but it is to provide everyone the facts to understand that I believe this president will continue to hit obstacles if he tries to use the executive branch in that way.

JW: Another possibility our friends worry about is the day after Republicans lose the election, Trump will claim fraud and then would call on MAGA groups to stage big protests in front of state capitals in swing states to stop the certification of test results, sort of a mini January 6th in various states. What do you think about that?

SP: I mean, the one thing I’ll say is that the president’s voter suppression agenda is deeply unpopular with the vast majority of the American people, including people that may not support progressive or Democratic causes. And so, I think it’s important that we not give the president more power in our minds than he really has. This is a fringe type of movement that he is seeking to aid and abet and strengthen. But this is a deeply unpopular movement in a world where people were really seeking to deprive the American people of their choice through staging these types of protests through trying to endanger certification. I think that you have to look at what happened with his off-cycle redistricting. It turns out that two can tango. And so, if that is the type of thing that MAGA groups might do in red states, I think you could expect that there wouldn’t be a reason for blue states to certify any Republican that won. If this is, in fact, the kind of fire that the president wants to play with there. I don’t have inside knowledge on that. But that is my suspicion. And that is what we have seen happen with respect to off cycle redistricting. He tried to do this complete off cycle redistricting, and you saw blue states say, well, we can do that too. And the United States Supreme Court, by the way, did not intervene to stop California’s new map. And so, I do think that this is something that’s quite messy for the president. If he tries to engage like this.

JW: The biggest danger is probably in the blue cities, in the red states, where Republican governors and Republican state attorneys general will cooperate with whatever Trump wants to do to reduce Democratic voting. For example, your home state of Texas, the governors, Greg Abbott, the state attorney general, Ken Paxton. But this is a place where Kamala Harris got 800,000 votes in 2024 in Dallas, 500,000 votes in Houston, 400,000 votes in Austin. There’s a lot of Democratic votes in Texas. But the Republican governor and the Republican state attorney general, I doubt they’re going to be like Brad Raffensperger in Georgia defying Trump in 2020. What do you say to that?

SP: First of all, I think we do have to see how this plays out. I mean, you’ve already seen the secretary of state in Texas raise deep concerns about the accuracy of the information that’s coming from the federal government. And that is not a person that is aligned with Democratic or progressive causes.But the other thing that’s important for people to understand is that the state and local governments do have a lot of authority. And you have in Texas, strong places like Harris County, which is where Houston, Texas, is, that are led by people that want to make sure that their citizens are able to vote, and they’re not going to stand idly by while the president or the governor or anyone else tries to undermine those votes so that that type of action could look like legal action, depending on what happens and depending on what mechanisms are used, it could look like blue states across the country also saying look, if this is how red state governors are going to act about blue cities, we can act that way about red cities. You have that in California. You have a number of places in California that are more red than blue, even though California is known as a blue state. Same with New York.So again, I think that this is going to require a multi-pronged effort for all people, first of all, to make sure they’re voting, make sure they’re registered to vote and to vote, and to turn out for the lawyers to be ready to bring the action that needs to happen. And for political actors, for people that hold these positions, to not give in to a voter suppression agenda, that may mean doing what happened in Georgia, where Republicans did defy the president, but it also may mean blue states having to step up and say, “we’re not going to allow the red states to try to cheat the American people out of an election.” We have some power here, too, and I think you’ll see all of that. And I think we have seen all of that over the course of the last year, I think off cycle. The redistricting remains a really good example.

JW: Of course, there are a lot of groups working on election protection. In many ways, the lead over the past year has been taken by the blue state attorneys general, led by, you know, Tish James in New York, Rob Bonta in California. They sued Trump every week, and they’ve been planning this since before he was elected. And of course, there’s the ACLU, the Brennan Center, the Legal Defense Fund of the NAACP. They’ve been planning election defense since Trump was elected. And then there’s the organizations whose leaders work with you on that Senate task force. You mentioned Marc Elias of Democracy docket. There’s also Vanita Gupta of NYU, Ian Basson, Protect Democracy, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders. How does your group, how does the Senate task force, coordinate this big array of very talented groups of very talented people?

SP: There’s a range of coordination. There’s a range of wonderful task force. It’s wonderful that the Senate task Force has gotten some attention publicly. There’s also been public reports, and we’ve been engaged with the House of Representatives that have been running scenarios. There are a number of election protection tables and organizations. So, people are in really close contact. This is a multi-pronged effort because you have threats to our elections that are coming in an unprecedented fashion from our president. And there’s a playbook that has to be run to defend against those threats. You also have threats that have always existed in American society. People across the country, in some of these areas that do not want individuals to be able to vote, that want to try to intimidate. There have been voter protection hotlines run by civil rights and pro voting organizations for years. And so those organizations are, of course, strengthening their efforts. And don’t forget that there’s also the candidates. We don’t do a lot of candidate work at Democracy Forward because we’re nonpartisan and we are just, we’re about everybody voting. But when you look at someone like a Marc Elias, I mean, he typically represents a lot of candidates who if someone is going to mess with their election results they’re going to be lawyered up and they’re going to bring cases against that as well. And so, the candidates and the parties are another piece of this, even if they have to exist in a separate sort of orbit or ecosystem, then the pro voting and nonprofit organization groups. So, this has been an incredibly coordinated effort so far. You’ve seen an incredible amount of coordination that a Democracy Forward, we’ve been able to drive against the Trump administration’s other actions across the board. And I think you’re going to see the lawyers be very coordinated this time as well.

JW: I want to ask specifically about Democracy Forward your group. RFK Jr. coauthored an op ed in The Wall Street Journal recently complaining about you. He said that in 2025, your organization filed more than 150 lawsuits and took more than 400 legal actions against the Trump administration and launched more than 250 public records investigations. Is there any truth to these charges?

SP: Yes. I mean, look, we are proud of that record. We’re disappointed that this moment of history requires that amount of litigation against the federal government, which is a government that is supposed to be serving the people. And so, we’re very disappointed. Any time we have to sue a federal or state or local government, that for us, that means that there are people in communities across this country that are being failed by their government and that have to take legal action. So, in that way, it is disappointing. But we do assure, we said this right out back in our response to The Wall Street Journal, we are very proud of our record to represent people and communities in the court. And that particular op ed, he was complaining about litigation that our organization is maintaining on behalf of cities and nonprofit organizations to defend the Affordable Care Act and health care for over 2.2 million people in the country. Right after he came out with his op ed, we won a big court order stopping the administration from undermining the ACA. He was trying to pretend as if somehow the administration was protecting the ACA. I mean, it was just a bit bonkers. So, we’re very proud of that record and stand by those numbers.

JW: You’ve launched a project called “100 Days of Action” for the rest of between now and Election Day. Tell us about that.

SP: So, this is really the most important thing I think, that people and communities can do before Election Day. There is the doom scrolling. There is thinking about all the different ways the election could be rigged, or that the president could try to overtake the election. And people in communities have to know that the lawyers are going to be there. The president is going to continue to lose in court, and that we are all going to have to band together to make sure that our elections do occur, and that people are able to vote and that their votes are counted. The most important thing, however, is not to get all drawn up into every way the election could go wrong, or to wonder about what type of legal action the lawyers are to file. Guess what? We’re all going to file them there. It’s to make sure that we all, as individuals are doing our part to make our voices heard in this election. And so, what that looks like is taking individual actions that are in many instances, are very simple to take that do not take much time between now and the election. And so, we are encouraging people this week as part of the action plan to go check your voter registration. You can do it online. You can get some information, make sure you’re registered to vote. Talk to your community. We want to make sure people are also being informed. And so, we have some great short, not long, but great reading material about how we got into this and what do people need to understand? Our communities are really important. Democracy is a kitchen table issue. And so, the “100 Days of Action” plan will include ways to take small steps within our individual communities to make sure that we’re strengthening our bonds, because this is a time when all Americans are having to come together in new ways. And we’ve seen that over the past year, but we’re really pleased to be able to help folks that we hear from every day who are saying, what can I do in this moment to really be able to help folks engage?

JW: And one last thing. Apparently, the 400 legal actions you’ve taken against the Trump administration last year didn’t keep you busy because you also wrote a book. It’s being published August 25th. It’s called Ordinary People Extraordinary Times. How to reclaim your power, fight for freedom and reimagine democracy. A guide for all of us. Briefly tell us what we’re going to find in this book when it’s published.

SP: I hope you find everything you need about how to plug in and engage in this time, at a time where history is going to look back. Our kids are going to look back and ask, what did those people do at a time when democracy, when the very existence of our communities, were under attack, how did we come together and not just defend, not just try to restore old systems, but to reimagine and create something that truly serves everyone? So, this is a book that comes out in paperback. It’s available in audiobook, very accessible. The proceeds from the book go to benefit the work of Democracy Forward. There are seven action steps, checklist tip sheets, very accessible, a website you can go to get more information. And it’s all about how people – what people can do in this time. I draw from the amazing stories of the cases that we have built on behalf of people and communities, the bravery we’ve seen in communities from ordinary people, as well as what our history has taught us about the role of ordinary people. People forget change in this country has never come from the top. It’s always come from the people, the people demanding more. And that’s the kind of demand that people need to make in this time. And we’ve all got to get to work.

JW: You’ve said many times that in November we are going to have free and fair elections. How come you’re so confident about that?

SP: I’m confident in the American people. I’m confident in the American people’s lawyers, and I’m confident in the way this country has found its way forward over the past year. At a time when hope is really hard to find, when fear simmers everywhere. We have seen people in communities come together in truly extraordinary ways. Hundreds of millions of people are disapproving of what’s happening in this country. We’ve seen millions of people on the streets in the No Kings protest and demonstrations. These are the largest, the largest single day, peaceful mobilizations of people in U.S. history. More people in this country have been trained in nonviolent, nonviolent, direct, collective action in this time than ever were trained even in the civil rights movement and the courts. Even with the Supreme Court, the courts have been serving as a guardrail as well. And so, all of those things together make me know that we are going to have free and fair elections, but we’re not going to have them automatically. We’re going to have them because of the actions and the work that individual people have to take every day. And that’s why we’re so excited to have this “100 Days of Action.” I’m excited to be talking to you. The book comes out to help people figure out how to engage, but we’re going to be able to do it.

JW: Skye Perryman of Democracy Forward. Her book, coming out in August, is Ordinary People, Extraordinary Times. Skye, thanks for all your work and thanks for talking with us today.

SP: Thank you.[BREAK]JW: The big movie this week–this month–this season–is Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey. Elon Musk’s view is that the film is “part of a left wing plan” to “destroy Western civilization”– This is a quote—“and everything that helped create it.” For our analysis, we turn to John Powers. He’s critic at large for Fresh Air with Terry Gross, where he has an audience of millions. John Powers, welcome back.

JP: I’m glad to be here, Jon.

JW: I understand you saw The Odyssey the way Christopher Nolan intended — in real IMAX, on a screen, 101 feet wide, 75 feet tall, and, of course, three hours long, bigger than anything previously known to moviegoers. What did you think? Was Elon Musk onto something when he said that Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey was “part of a left wing plan” to “destroy Western civilization”?

JP: Well, that’s probably extreme, but I actually know what he’s saying. The complaint is that it’s a woke version of the Odyssey. And there’s kind of the dumb version of that, which is to look at a couple of the casting choices, like Lupita Nyong’o, and say, “but she was supposed to be white”–when, of course, the problem with casting Helen of Troy always is that she’s never beautiful enough. Charlize Theron in the film is an exceedingly beautiful woman, but if you made her Helen of Troy, she’s not beautiful enough. But by putting an African, a black African actress, in the role, what you do is you make her different and exotic enough that you can believe the people there all think she’s the most beautiful person in the world. Perfectly reasonable casting, not some sort of woke nonsense.The part that’s true, I guess, in what he’s saying–not that it’s destroying Western civilization–is that the Odyssey had Greek values about winning and losing in conquest and slaves and kings–all the sorts of things that one can imagine Elon Musk liking, because no doubt he, in some sad yet grandiose way, fancies himself a kind of Odysseus, which is the person who’s much smarter and deserves to rule because he’s so much cleverer.And here the Odysseus, played by Matt Damon, is kind of doleful and regretful of the things he’s done in order to win, feeling that he’s destroying civilization. So if you’re Musk, you’re thinking that this version is kind of the anti-Trump version, which is it’s not about winning. It’s about feeling bad even though you won.

JW: Yeah. The way Maureen Dowd put that was “he’s an action hero who feels bad about being an action hero.” And it’s striking that Christopher Nolan has pretty much the same character in most of his movies. Oppenheimer, the last one, invented the bomb to bring an immediate end to a war that had lasted way too long, and then he himself suffered psychologically afterward when he realized the damage the bomb had done to ordinary Japanese women and children. And Christopher Nolan’s Odysseus invents the Trojan horse to end a war that had lasted way too long, but then he himself suffered psychologically when he realized the damage it had done to the women and children of Troy — who were, of course, raped and murdered by his own men. So Christopher Nolan gives us two guys suffering from a kind of PTSD, 3000 years apart.

JP: I mean, I guess if you’re being nasty, you’re saying they’re all doleful. If you are a fan–I’m not a particular Christopher Nolan fan–but if you give him credit for having an intention, his stories, including Batman, are all about people who set out to do things that are good and make the world safe and better and put together, and wind up doing things that they wind up regretting. Because, in fact, what looks like success always ends up being tinged with failure and loss and as a vision of the world. you know that. I mean, that’s a perfectly reasonable vision of the world, better than Rocky movies, better than lots of other things, probably politically at this moment in time. Better than the vision that says winning is all that matters. Go in and do what you want.So destroying Troy and feeling bad about it when you realize you’re destroying civilization, that doesn’t seem to me to be a contemptible vision of the world to be offering, particularly at this point in history, where it’s clear that he, like many other people, feel that civilization is collapsing, that the norms of decency and responsibility are lost, that ideas of hospitality are being shattered.So that part of — even I think some of the casting in this film, which is which has been attacked for being like DEI casting, is actually about making films hospitable to people who are different. So for all of those things, I just think it’s unfair to suggest it’s just doleful.Now it is doleful. The disappointment for me in it is that I would want him to have all those regrets and still be the more charming, fun, clever Odysseus that I loved and that both Elon Musk and I identify with.

JW: The people who read Homer have a lot of complaints. In many ways, it’s not the job of the filmmaker to make an “accurate” recreation of the book, but there are opportunities in the story that Homer tells, which Christopher Nolan chose to pass up. One of the more interesting ones that’s been brought up by the Homer scholars is there’s no sex in this movie. Whereas in Greek mythology, there’s a lot of sex that gods are always having sex with each other. They’re jealous.Odysseus has been away from his wife Penelope, first for the ten years of the war and then ten years coming home. It’s been a long time with no sex. In Homer’s book, there’s a lot of sex. For example, the critics talk about the Cerce part. She’s the witch who turns his men into pigs. In Homer’s story, she kind of bewitches Odysseus and has sex with him every night for a year. And it’s kind of a lot of fun. It’s exciting. In the movie, this is the character played by Samantha Morton. Maureen Dowd says Samantha Morton plays this part “like a vindictive feminist hippie making ceramic pots in Vermont.”

JP: Maureen always being nasty, whereas I was actually thinking it’s more accurately described as –interesting that two of the people who translated the Odyssey, both Daniel Mendelsohn and Emily Wilson, both actually referred to her as kind of “earthy” rather than hippie. She is given some slightly strident things to say, probably modern, strident things to say.

JW: Yes. Let me just underline that: she says that she turned the men into pig– by the way, in kind of a horror movie scene where she kind of rips them their bodies and reshapes them, which is nothing like what happens in Homer and Homer. She just taps them with her magic wand. And then she tells Odysseus “they raped and pillaged across the world for you, filthy soldiers with empty bellies and hot blood. Look at them and know your own men,” she says, pointing at the pigs. This is pure Christopher Nolan. There’s nothing like that in Homer.

JP: No. So? Here, Christopher Nolan, because it’s a big pop thing and in fact is over-explicit and has all sorts of failings that one would expect of a big pop spectacle. Like there’s too much action. There’s a scene where there’s a great scene with the Cyclops, played by Bill Irwin. I think it’s a very good.

JW: I love the Cyclops episode.

JP: Okay, it’s a good scene, but then there’s a scene with these kind of larger than life metal clad monsters, the Laestrygonians. And it’s just there, I think, for action. It’s the one thing in the film–I mean, I think anything else in the film, I can understand why it’s there, but that just seems like it’s just there to have action. And Christopher Nolan loves action.The film builds to the final showdown with Odysseus and the suitors. And I was joking with my girlfriend, I had not realized that Odysseus was also John Wick — because he kills so many people in such a confined space, so implausibly, with arrows in his back and all the rest, that that really is absurd.There are those flaws, but maybe you think those are the flaws that allow you to tell this particular story at this point in history, because they’re the audience that will go for that, and then learn and learn the Odyssey story and will actually learn maybe the lesson that he wants to impart about civilization and not just being, not just winning and all the rest. So, I mean, in defending it, if Christopher Nolan was bringing out his new translation of The Odyssey from Cambridge University Press, then I could reasonably understand why Greek scholars would complain. But given that it’s a blockbuster that has to make the money back, It has to play in every country of the world, I would probably say, even though it pains me to say: he’s done a really good job of doing that, doing a mass market spectacle.

JW: The biggest disappointment for me was not the absence of sex, it was the sirens. I was really looking forward to seeing what’s he going to do with the Sirens– You know, the most legendary girl group in Western civilization. Homer says their song is irresistible to any man who hears it. And so our man Matt Damon has himself tied to the mast and has wax in the ears of his crew so they won’t be drawn to the Sirens. And then we see his face, and he’s writhing in pain like he’s being forced to listen to, I don’t know, heavy metal at high volume or something like that. But we don’t get to hear the Sirens.

JP: Let me ask you this: Can you think of a composer anywhere in the world capable of writing that music?

JW: Let me just say there is a better version, which is, strangely enough, the Coen Brothers movie of the Odyssey, O brother, where Art thou? Their scene with the sirens has Emmylou Harris, Alison Krauss and Gillian Welch singing some 19th century beautiful folk song in harmony, and it is kind of wonderful and bewitching. And you want to hear it again.

JP: I understand, but I mean, as I recall, O brother, where Art thou? Isn’t set in in ancient Greece.

JW: No, it’s set in like Mississippi in the ‘30s.

JP: Yes. Right. Exactly. You know I think it’s not a very good scene. I agree with you. I think I think you would probably need to have some music, and you would have to find some way with the camera and the poetry of filmmaking to make it come more alive than it did, because I think that’s just a disappointing scene. I can imagine he got hours and hours of his — He has a very good composer, his composer, trying to do the thing.It’s very much like in Proust where, you know, there’s the tiny phrase that Swann loves in Swann’s Way. And whenever they’ve tried to make movies of it, you’re then always stuck with the fact they don’t. It’s supposed to be this one little phrase of music that haunts you forever. That’s a hard thing to write. It’s easy to write an earworm. You know, you could get Barry Manilow to write it. I was joking that probably he wanted Taylor Swift to do the to do the Siren thing.But and there are a huge number of critics, almost all of my friends of him think of him as like a great filmmaker. And what I think he’s great at certain things. I think he’s an excellent storyteller. I think he’s unbelievably good at weaving together complicated narratives and braiding them so that you can always follow them. I think he’s actually good at playing with time. I think he edits exceedingly well. I think in terms of visually, I think I always think it’s duller than I think it’s going to be. It’s not as exciting. And I think there’s some sort of level of poetry he can’t quite get to. And even in the action scenes, I don’t think he’s as good as, say, Kathryn Bigelow. I was thinking if you gave Kathryn Bigelow $250 million and said, really give us a scary scene with a Cyclops, she could do as well. Although the Cyclops with the Bill Irwin thing is very, very good. But I just don’t think that somehow I have that sense of him as a genius filmmaker.If I can just add one more thought here, because this is part of part of the story, is that the reason why it’s already made $650 million around the world is that Nolan has been singled out in a way, perhaps like Stanley Kubrick earlier, as the guy who’s the master of filmmaking. So he has the loyal audience who will always go. And a year in advance by the Imax 70 millimeter version. And there’s a weird fetish of the technique with him.

Speaker 3: Yes, yes.

JP: —and which you also had with Kubrick, where you where people are saying Kubrick was such a perfectionist. Everything had to be perfect, they said. Yeah, except he shot Vietnam in England, except for that. And it didn’t look like Vietnam. Except for that. He’s a perfectionist, but the point is he I think he is not a great soaring filmmaker, but he’s excellent at other things.

JW: What did you think of the ending where Matt Damon gives the crown to his son and heads off into the sunset with Anne Hathaway, a kind of aging couple headed for a quiet retirement?

JP: There’s an article out in the Atlantic now, which I haven’t read, but it’s been mentioned to me about how it’s a Christian movie, not a Greek movie. And there is the huge atonement level of the confessional thing and being forgiven for your sins. And this is very much part of it. And once again, this is part, you know, you can go it’s not it’s not just Elon Musk, although I will be happy to abuse him anytime we can.You know, if you go all the way back to, say, Nietzsche, perhaps Nietzsche’s favorite character in all the world was Odysseus, and he loved him for being a liar and for being alive and being able to shift himself so much. So Nietzsche and Musk would both think, you have this guy who’s charismatic and smart and a great warrior and a great thinker and all these sort of things, and he turns himself into a kind of willful retiree, which, of course, he wouldn’t have been, as we know from the kind of people who become kings. They tend not to sail off and give it up. You know, Joe Biden, who I think is a long way from Odysseus, did not get on the boat with Jill and go to the western islands.

JW: On the Christian front, there’s a similar argument made by the New York Times conservative political columnist David French. In disagreeing with Musk, he calls the movie, “one of the most conservative movies I’ve ever seen. The moral of the movie is yes, there are universal moral laws, and this is what happens when prideful men believe they know more than God.”

JP: Yes. No it is. That’s true.

JW: But in the movie, the God is Zeus, who is a little bit different from the Christian god.

JP: But we are post-Zeus. And so now today’s modern conservative believes in the Judeo-Christian tradition. And probably more likely than not the Christian tradition rather than the Judeo-Christian tradition. Although they keep the Judeo around, you know.

JW: The vengeful God works for them.

JP: Yeah. The vengeful God works. You know, they like that part of it. But it is a strange thing. It’s it is both conservative and, on the other hand, you could say it’s kind of –because many of the reviews I’ve read have talked about — you can you can see the destruction of Vietnam or other countries in what was going on in this.

JW: And. And it is the Westerners who take their armies and their strategies to the East. And destroy the East, because of their hubris.

JP: Yes. And it is attempting to suggest that women are also among the colonized people. There’s a funny thing, I think, I believe, in the Emily Wilson review, where she points out that there’s a character played by John Leguizamo, who’s a swineherd, who is constantly being described as Odysseus’s “servant,” and kind of friendly servant. And as Emily Wilson points out, the term is “slave”. You know that they keep calling them servants when in fact, yes, but except for you’re a servant, but I do own you. But people would find that disturbing.There’s all the complexity of stuff. There’s the complexity, the fact that we like Odysseus, yet his men rape and murder. And he’s cool with that. that he wants to be king. That he will he will kill all the suitors. He does think up the Trojan horse. And yet at the same time, we like him. But he also likes to sleep with these attractive kind of witchy women.It’s just a Christopher Nolan, I guess, artistic blind spot. There are just certain directors who, when they get around sex, even if they want to, they kind of freeze up and can’t do it. I just have that feeling that he’s good at lots of things, but when you go into that arena, he never feels particularly comfortable with it.So it’s pretty fun to take drugs and have sex with Charlize Theron. I think huge parts of the audience would think, “man, he’s got it made. You know, I’m not going home either.”

JW: John, your closing thoughts.

JP: When you’re reading certain critics, we’re like experts in this. I’m reminded how there was a, I think maybe Entertainment Weekly or maybe it was the LA Times someplace used to run a thing where there’d be– If there was a movie about firemen, they’d get a fireman to review it. And the firemen would always find 8 million things that weren’t accurate about it, and couldn’t actually see what was going on.And I feel with certain of the Greek experts, they seem not to realize that they are watching something that wasn’t designed to be an attempt to recapture what Greeks thought. It’s not a historical investigation, but it’s an attempt to try to bring to life for an existing audience in a modern version, the same thing.So yes, many of the complaints are true. And there are things I don’t like about the film, but I think the one thing that seems unfair is to suggest that Christopher Nolan didn’t spend all this money to show us what Greeks actually thought in the time of an epic. That’s just a crazy thing to think.

JW: John Powers–You can listen to his reviews at NPR’s Fresh Air with Terry Gross. John, thanks for talking with us today.

JP: My pleasure.

news.title: To win over working class voters, Democrats need to stop talking about democracy
news.text:
There's an active debate in Democratic politics between progressives and moderates about how to build a winning coalition.

A new report from a pair of California researchers, shared exclusively with NPR, argues that debate misses the point. The answer isn't centrism, they write, it's respect for where working-class voters are coming from.

"It's about understanding that people need a sense of personal and economic security before they will support the changes progressives are calling for," the authors write.

The report's authors are, to put a label on it, college-educated coastal elites. Joan C. Williams is a law professor from San Francisco who is known for her work in diversity equity and inclusion. Jared Abbott leads the Center for Working Class Politics and has a PhD from Harvard. Their intended audience is people who share their progressive politics.

Their message is that the Democratic Party would be making a huge mistake if it keeps catering to social justice warriors and fails to understand, respect and appeal to working-class voters. "The path heavily favors the party that wins working-class voters," the report explains.

"I am tired of losing," Williams said in an interview. "I want to build a sustained progressive coalition capable of delivering on progressive goals. And that's not what we have now and that's not what we've had for decades."

Titled "The Left's Coalition Crisis: Understanding the Massive Divide Between Working Class and College Educated Voters, and How to Bridge It," the report argues Democrats have lost support from working-class voters of all races because the party's base is out of touch with the priorities and values of those Americans.

"Until Democrats understand the importance of really respecting, listening to and taking seriously the values of self-reliance, the values of patriotism and tradition and personal security," Abbott said, "they're going to have a major messaging and a major electoral problem."

Abbott and Williams define the working class as people without a four year college degree, earning from $40,000 to $100,000 a year — the middle 50% of American incomes.

"If progressives want to build working-class support, they need to connect with people whose top priorities are paychecks, prices and personal safety," the report states.

The authors offer a two-part prescription to "develop the cultural competence to bridge the diploma divide."

"First, consistently embrace a populism that decries a rigged economy where hard work fails to yield a stable middle class life," it states.

Then, "rigorously avoid reinforcing right populism's narrative that liberal college grads look down on Americans without college degrees."

The report relies on the results from the Class Gaps Poll, a survey of more than 5,000 Americans conducted earlier this year.

It finds there's a disconnect between the priorities of college-educated liberals and those of working-class voters on issues like LGBTQ+ rights, abortion access, climate change, immigration and income redistribution.

The greatest divide is on the issue of "resisting authoritarianism."

"Resisting authoritarianism is the second highest priority for liberal college grads but for workers, it's like 19 out of 20," said Williams.

Defending democracy was a major theme of Vice President Kamala Harris's losing presidential campaign in 2024. She delivered her closing argument from the White House Ellipse recounting President Trump's actions on January 6, 2021.

Another major theme of her campaign was defending abortion access. Those are two issues, according to the report, "that liberal college grads prioritize but most working-class Americans don't."

The lesson, they argue, isn't that working-class voters are unreachable. It's that you can't reach them if you're not focused on the issues they care about the most.

"If we really care about stopping authoritarianism, if we really care about defending democracy, we have to stop talking about defending democracy in the way that we've been doing for the last too many years," Abbott said.

So, what should Democrats be talking about? The economy, and not just in abstract terms like "affordability," because wages are as important as costs, the researchers find.

"Ten out of 12 workers' top priorities are economics, so if you want them to vote for you, talk about economics," Williams said.

Abbott said Democratic candidates this midterm election year have done a relatively good job of keeping that economic focus. But how they talk about economic issues matters too.

The researchers took issues that weren't top priorities for working-class voters and poll-tested new messages framed around working-class values. That shift in messaging was able to move opinion.

"If you care passionately about climate change, and I do, the answer is to tie it to something working-class folks do care about," Williams said.

When they framed climate initiatives around creating jobs, addressing rising energy costs, reducing pollution and countering China, they got much more support from working-class voters than asking if they support "major investments in energy efficiency and cleaner power to reduce pollution and address the climate crisis even if this raises the cost of energy a little."

But the paper warns, working-class reframing only works if it comes from a genuine place of trying to reach across the class divide or it risks being seen as elites trying to manipulate non-elites.

Notably, Abbott says, reframing most issues didn't drive down support from college-educated liberals.

"In general, we found that there are no clear systematic tradeoffs, that what's better messaging for the working class is typically better messaging for all voters," Abbott said.
news.summary: Working class voters have moved away from the Democratic Party. Winning them back is key to the party's future, a new reports shows. But first, the messaging has to change.

news.title: Will Graham Platner supporters back Troy Jackson in Maine Senate race?
news.text:
Rachel Flehinger was disappointed and frustrated when oyster farmer Graham Platner withdrew his name as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine after an allegation of sexual assault he denies.

Flehinger, 50, of Portland, Maine, and the founder of community activism group ActivateMaine, felt Platner was “canceled” by the Democratic Party before proper legal investigations of the allegations were conducted. She has known Platner since before he ran for office, she told USA TODAY, and found that he was always supportive and inclusive.

As someone with post-traumatic stress disorder, Flehinger also thinks he was unfairly judged for some of his past behavior. (Platner has apologized for controversial Reddit posts, including those in which he asked "Why don’t black people tip?" and said that sexual assault victims should "take some responsibility," saying he made them when he had PTSD and depression after leaving the military.)

But for all her disappointment, Flehinger said she will “1000%” vote for Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate President who officially replaced Platner as the Democratic nominee on July 25.

"He stands on progressive policies," she said.

"I am ‘Anyone But Collins,’ but I think Troy stands with me on the issues I care about," Flehinger said, referring to Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, whom Jackson will face in November.

Many Platner supporters like Flehinger are hurt and disappointed. Some of them felt betrayed by Platner himself, while others don’t believe the accusations against him, find the timing suspicious or think there was more to the story.

For some, their anger is directed at the Democratic Party: Karen Heck, former mayor of Waterville, Maine, and a Platner supporter, said she is “sick to death of the establishment Democrats who were threatened by the energy Graham unleashed" and is planning to unenroll from the party.

Yet many remain committed to what they see as the movement Platner launched, starting with defeating Collins, which could be the key to Democrats’ hopes of taking control of the U.S. Senate.

Ryan Warren, a 43-year-old from Fairfield, Maine, who volunteered for Platner’s campaign since August 2025, said he felt uncertain and a sense of grief when the sexual assault allegation broke July 6 in Politico. But the principles he believes in, which include health care as a right, affordable housing and a minimum tax on billionaires, are bigger than just one candidate, he said. 

"There was a lot of confusion and mixed emotions two weeks ago. If our movement was only about a candidate or an astroturf trend, we would have been sunk," Warren, now the organizer of a network of Platner's volunteers that want to keep his policies alive, said in an email to USA TODAY. "Most everyone I’ve spoken to, whatever their concerns about the recent past or the future of our movement, sees that Troy Jackson has worked hard for those principles, is genuinely committed to them."

Will Platner fans support Jackson?

In some ways, Jackson was the heir apparent to Platner, an oyster farmer from Sullivan, a coastal town just north of Bar Harbor. Jackson is a logger from Allagash, a tiny town almost as far north as you can go in Maine. 

“He has the experience of being among people,” Flehinger said. “In the same way Graham had oystermen, he had loggers.” 

Platner was formerly endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, as was Jackson in the Democratic gubernatorial primary he lost to Hannah Pingree. Platner and Jackson had endorsed each other before the primary. After Platner’s July 8 withdrawal announcement, Our Revolution, the grassroots political action organization born out of Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign, endorsed Jackson.

University of New Hampshire Survey Center Director Andy Smith said in an interview that Jackson is “Graham Platner with a record," meaning Jackson has previously served in elected office, unlike Platner, but the two men have similar progressive, economically populist ideologies. On the other hand, Jackson lacks Platner's charismatic speaking style, Smith noted.

Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, told USA TODAY in early July that Jackson would be the "closest thing to Platner in terms of his populism, on being critical of corporations, emphasizing labor unions."

Indeed, Flehinger said when she started looking at the possible candidates to replace Platner, she realized Jackson was the most closely aligned with her. Warren said he’s "excited" to vote for Jackson.

“His commitment to popular policies that help ordinary Mainers, I don't think his commitment to those ideas has been challenged by anybody, you know. I think he's been standing by workers for decades,” Warren said in an interview with USA TODAY. “He has the commitment to the right policies that will be good for Mainers, and I think that he has the legislative experience and ability to build coalitions to get things done.”

Jackson started his career as a Republican who opposed abortion and gay marriage, but is now a progressive Democrat who has received high scores from abortion and LGBTQ groups. There have been reports that he had a temper when he ran the state Senate.

But Flehinger, who runs a community organizing group called ActivateMaine, thinks it's admirable that he changed and said that they don’t have the luxury of looking for “perfect people” anymore.

Or will they spurn the party?

Maine voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election by nearly seven points, but Collins has won five terms in the state thanks to her moderate voting record. She's the only Republican senator to represent a Harris-won state, and this year, winning her seat is a key priority for Democrats as they hope to flip four GOP seats and take the majority in the Senate.

A poll from UNH Survey Center found that 51% of those who voted for Platner chose Jackson as their first choice for his replacement. Jackson drew his strongest support from self-described socialists (72%) and progressives (60%). 

Yet it also found that Democrats aren’t as united behind him as Republicans are behind Collins: 88% of Democrats say they will vote for him, as opposed to 99% of Republicans who say they will support Collins. 4% of Democrats and 2% of Independents said they are considering another candidate, and 2% and 10% respectively aren’t sure.

Smith thinks that in the end, Democrats will coalesce around Jackson. Typically, party members will fall back in line when an election arrives, and Smith thinks that will be especially true in a midterm year when Democrats are angry.

“They're going to end up voting for the Democratic nominee, no matter who that is,” Smith said. “They're mad as hell, and they're going to get out and vote. And this vote for the Democratic candidate for Senate is essentially a vote against Trump.”

Flehinger said that many of her peers who support Platner are disillusioned. Warren was frustrated with the Maine Democratic Party's attitude after the sexual assault allegations became public, saying it felt condescending toward his supporters. Meanwhile, Flehinger objected to the party's accusation that Platner was trying to put his "thumb on the scale" in selecting a new candidate, an allegation his campaign denied.

Heck is planning on leaving the party but said she will still vote against Collins this election. Flehinger said there are a lot of “ABC” people—anyone but Collins—and Warren thinks that people will “vote strategically.” 

“Some people feel this way, some people feel that way, right?” Warren said. “So I think that there are people who will be hurt and who will enjoy other things about the beauty that Maine has to offer in the fall instead of knocking doors. I think in terms of people's personal convictions that we will come together and we will vote strategically to defeat Susan Collins in the fall.”

Despite their disappointment, Warren and Flehinger don’t want Platner’s movement to die with his campaign.

“I don't think that it serves anybody to quit politics," Flehinger said. “I think it's our responsibility to stay there and keep voting and keep trying to change the system.”

news.title: Gavin Newsom Affair Resurfaces as Ex-Aide Breaks 20-Year Silence and Reveals Kamala Harris' Advice
news.text: Breaking two decades of silence, a woman who had a high-profile romantic affair with Gavin Newsom revealed that Kamala Harris privately stepped in to urge her to stay completely quiet just as the explosive 2007 political scandal initially broke out.Ruby Rippey, 54, published her first-person account on Tuesday in a Vanity Fair essay, landing as both Newsom and Harris weigh 2028 presidential runs. The timing turns a scandal many viewed as settled into a live question about power, workplace conduct, and how the party's two biggest names handled it.The Advice That Kept Her QuietRippey worked as Newsom's appointments secretary when he was mayor of San Francisco. She was also married to Alex Tourk, his campaign manager and close friend. She writes that the affair began in the summer of 2005, during a period when she was struggling with alcohol and cocaine addiction.When the scandal became public in 2007, Rippey says Harris, then the city's district attorney, called her. Broke, unemployed, and weighing a memoir offer, Rippey recalls Harris telling her to 'just pause' because more time would give her 'better perspective'. She now calls it the best advice she received and stayed largely silent for years.A Boss, a Secretary and the Power BetweenRippey does not allege coercion, but she frames the relationship around the imbalance between a mayor and his subordinate. 'Power does not need to coerce. It only needs to exist,' she writes, adding that the duty to hold the line sat with the person who held the power. She says she owns her choices while insisting the greater responsibility was his.She says the 2017 #MeToo movement reshaped how she understood what happened. For Newsom, she writes, the affair reads as a footnote. For her, it split her life into a before and an after.Newsom's Account Under FireMuch of the essay disputes how Newsom described events in his own memoir, published earlier this year. He called it the 'briefest of affairs' and 'the worst betrayal' of his life, and said he 'came clean' to Tourk. Rippey counters that she had already confessed to her husband, and that Newsom's telling hands him credit for something she did.A spokesperson for Newsom, Izzy Gardon, said the governor acknowledged his role and apologised nearly two decades ago, met his wife, started a family, and has since focused on serving Californians. Gardon added that Newsom has nothing further to say.Why It Lands NowHarris has not publicly responded, and a representative did not comment when contacted. Both she and Newsom, 58, rose through California politics with early backing from former San Francisco mayor Willie Brown, and both have supported each other's ambitions over the years.That history now faces fresh scrutiny, and Newsom's private life is likely to draw sharper attention if he formally enters the race. Harris said in April she 'might' run in 2028. Newsom has said 'fate will determine' whether their careers collide. Rippey's essay makes certain that a 20-year-old scandal, and the way allies managed it, follows both of them into the race.

news.title: Israel's decades-old US support risks losing Democrats
news.text:
WASHINGTON, July 29 - For generations, support for Israel united Washington. Now Israel's attacks on Gaza, the Iran war and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close ties to U.S. Republicans are eroding Democratic backing, threatening to turn one of America's closest alliances into a partisan divide.

Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.

The shift is evident in Congress. This month, nearly half of House Democrats voted for a failed amendment to cut off aid to Israel, legislation that once likely would have been defeated by an overwhelming bipartisan majority. Israel receives $3.8 billion annually in U.S. military aid and received billions more in emergency funds in recent years.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and some of his lieutenants opposed the measure, calling it overly broad. But former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark were among those voting yes.

Democrats are increasingly divided over whether military aid should continue unchanged, be restricted to defensive weapons or be halted altogether.

U.S. Senator Chris Coons of Delaware, the leading Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he hopes Israeli elections in October help restore bipartisan U.S. support while opening a new chapter beyond Netanyahu's leadership.

"New governments get to change direction," Coons told Reuters, adding, "Netanyahu has kept Israel at war for years now, partly to avoid the political consequences of his choices."

Overall sentiment toward Israel is declining. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.

"Yes, there is a vigorous debate, but across broad segments of the parties, support for Israel remains firmly in the mainstream," said Danny Danon, Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, in an interview.

ISRAEL A FLASHPOINT IN MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC RACE

The shift faces a major test in Tuesday's Democratic U.S. Senate primary in Michigan where voters will weigh competing visions of U.S. support with growing numbers of congressional Democrats questioning longstanding U.S. military aid.

The race between progressive Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Representative Haley Stevens will determine who faces Republican Mike Rogers in November and reflects the wider Democratic debate over Israel and longstanding U.S. military support.

Stevens made a video with AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a major donor to her campaign, arguing that a close relationship with Israel "yields trade, that yields economic growth and that keeps our freedoms safe."

By contrast, El-Sayed, a former public health official, told Fox News: "The question is whether we want a politics where our money is sent over to Israel to fund genocide and apartheid instead of investing in our own kids."

A U.N. inquiry and several human rights groups have accused Israel of committing genocide in its military's devastation of Gaza, an allegation Israel rejects, saying it is fighting Hamas and taking steps to reduce civilian harm.

Israeli policy has been a factor in other battleground congressional races, including New York, Florida and Colorado.

DEMOCRATIC SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL ERODES

Strains with Democrats deepened 11 years ago, when in a speech to Congress at the request of the Republican majority Netanyahu attacked a deal crafted by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, on controlling Iran's nuclear program.

Sentiment critical of Israel grew after Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack, in which nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals were killed and hundreds were taken hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed, according to Gaza health officials.

Israel's bombardment of Gaza has reshaped Democratic politics, fueling a backlash among younger voters and deepening a generational divide within the party.

Campus protests in 2024 intensified pressure on Democrats to reassess support for Israel. Some analysts say President Joe Biden's refusal to do so contributed to Democratic nominee Kamala Harris' loss to Trump later that year.

Adding to tensions, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for Netanyahu's arrest for alleged war crimes.

This primary election cycle, some establishment candidates have been defeated by more progressive challengers who have questioned support for Israel, mostly in congressional districts dominated by Democrats.

Jeremy Ben-Ami, president of J Street, a progressive pro-Israel rival to AIPAC, said the debate within the Democratic Party reflected a backlash against the right-wing Netanyahu and AIPAC, calling it "a toxic brew that really has helped to make Israel, unfortunately, a real wedge issue in the Democratic Party."

AIPAC did not respond to requests for comment.

Shibley Telhami, a University of Maryland professor of government and politics and senior non-resident fellow at the Brookings Institution, called it a "paradigm shift that sees Israel now as a villain, even a genocidal villain, in a way that was never the case before."

While some conservative influencers have joined the attack, the Republican Party will support Israel as long as evangelical Christians and Trump stand firm, Telhami said in an interview.

ISRAEL RESHAPES POLITICAL BATTLEGROUNDS

The divide over Israel is spilling into congressional campaigns elsewhere.

Republican Representative Mike Lawler, who represents a district outside New York City with a large Jewish population, has used the Democratic shift on Israel to attack challenger Cait Conley in a battleground fight for control of the House.

In southern Florida, moderate Representative Jared Moskowitz, a consistent supporter of Israel aid, is being challenged in the August 18 Democratic primary by democratic socialist Oliver Larkin, who campaigns on his belief that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza and supports an immediate suspension of U.S. military aid to Israel.

Recent opinion polls show Moskowitz leading Larkin by 32 percentage points.

Longtime U.S. Representative Diana DeGette was defeated in the Colorado Democratic primary by Ethiopian-born Melat Kiros. Kiros has called for ending wars, including by stopping military aid to Israel, while DeGette said she supported sending only defensive weapons to Israel.

U.S. Senator Mazie Hirono, who has advocated for a two-state solution and more humanitarian aid for Palestinians, said, "I think the support for Israel's right to exist, all of that is there. It's just the (Israeli) leadership we seriously question." REUTERS

But when push comes to shove, the first guy will risk slamming into Fenway’s Green Monster to make a key catch. The other guy will play the best he is required, and as long as the checks cash, he doesn’t care if they are over or under 0.500. There are champions like Tom Brady and Michael Jordan. And then there are highly talented competitors who have won little to nothing. They play the whole season, they go through the motions, but oftentimes their goals are more personal than team-oriented. I remember Jalen Rose refusing to rejoin the Bulls in the playoffs after team doctors had cleared him to play. He claimed something about possibly harming his future earning potential (meaning commercials and shoes).

Politics today is rife with frauds and self-promoters. Gavin Newsom destroyed California so as to get a shot at running for president. The basic things like having nice roads and adding capacity to dams and reservoirs were too boring for Governor Hair. He was into overloading the state with illegal aliens and making gas and everything else prohibitively expensive. It was a bit of a joke when we went to Lake Tahoe for a couple of days. We stayed right near the Nevada-California line, and we always knew on which side we were by the price of gas as advertised. Kamala Harris can brag that she was a California attorney general and senator, vice president, and Democratic candidate for president. But, in truth, did she accomplish anything in those roles? Can someone tell me one law that she spearheaded in the Senate? Can somebody point out some initiative that she led as vice president that is still running today? JD Vance has been tasked with rooting out fraud from the federal budget and seems to be sinking his teeth into this job. What did VP Cackles accomplish with her border portfolio? While she, her boss, and their clueless spokesthing said that the border was closed, Fox drones showed thousands crossing over unfettered. Whom ya gonna believe? Them or your eyes? Harris was not elected through primaries but rather appointed by Joe Biden between naps. She has a resume to kill and accomplishments of a six-year-old.

The same can be said of many politicians, including AOC and Bernie Sanders. Anybody know of a signature law that AOC wrote and shepherded through the House and Senate? I know of no such thing. She scared away Amazon from her district and has shown that when she opens her mouth, she reveals how much space she has for rent in her brain. She is famous, has lots of online followers, and is becoming a household name. But, like Fauci, she is unaccomplished. Five-star General of the Army Dwight Eisenhower had a few medals on his chest; total loser “I’m going to warn the Chinese first” Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Mark Milley had half the weight of an Abrams tank stuck to his jacket, and he accomplished nothing. He presided over the death of 13 Marines in the uncontrolled egress from Kabul. They should melt his medals and sell the scrap iron to reduce the federal deficit.

One hundred and three Democrats voted in favor of Thomas Massie’s amendment to stop all military funding to Israel. These people ran in their districts, showed their accomplishments, and won their races. Do they not realize that if Israel ceases to exist, the Palestinians and their pals in the Muslim Brotherhood will not retire and say job well done? They will look to Europe and the U.S. as their next addresses for conquest. We hear strange things of late like Somalis built this country, or Muslims built New York. It’s all rubbish, but clearly the goal is to set the foundation for claiming, as Muslims always do, that some land is intrinsically theirs and must be redeemed from infidels — Jews and Christians alike. One doesn’t need to like Israel, but wishing that it goes away only means that your death and destruction have been moved up by six months. Israel, for some, is like that annoying seawall that ruins your views. If you could only get rid of it, you would not only have a great view of the sea, but the sea would gobble up your home and your belongings. Be careful for what you wish for. Most antisemites cut off their noses to spite their faces. Hitler could have had a nuclear bomb if he had not driven the likes of Edward Teller and Leo Szilard from Europe.

Fauci is to testify before Congress. No doubt he will invoke the Fifth Amendment and pull a Comey by not remembering a thing. He is the epitome of the credentialed class without the accomplishments to match the diplomas and awards.

news.text:

news.title: Ruby Rippey, former Gavin Newsom staffer, offers new details on their affair 20 years ago
news.text:
SAN FRANCISCO -- A former staffer who had an affair with Gavin Newsom more than 20 years ago offered extensive details in an essay published Tuesday by Vanity Fair, taking issue with how the California governor has more recently characterized what happened.

Newsom, then the mayor of San Francisco, admitted in 2007 that he had an affair in the years prior with Ruby Rippey, his appointments secretary and the wife of his campaign manager, Alex Tourk. Rippey has not spoken much about the scandal as Newsom has risen in politics and emerged as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

In the Vanity Fair piece, Rippey criticizes Newsom's description of the affair and its fallout in a memoir he published earlier this year. He wrote that it was the "briefest of affairs," and recounted how he "came clean" to Tourk, a close friend.

"That detail-subtle but significant-is the one that stays with me," Rippey wrote. "It reads-to me, at least-as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done."

Newsom had filed for divorce from his wife, former Fox News host Kimberly Guilfoyle, before the affair, but the relationship with his subordinate was an early political stumbling block for Newsom. Tourk resigned after confronting Newsom about it, and Newsom later held a news conference where he said, "Everything you've read is true and I'm deeply sorry for that."

Still, he was reelected later that year with over 73% of the vote.

"The Governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor," Newsom spokesperson Izzy Gardon said in a statement to CNN and KGO-TV/ABC7 Eyewitness News in San Francisco, responding to Rippey's essay.

"In the time since, he met his wife, started a family, and has focused on serving Californians. He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add," the statement said.

Newsom's personal life is likely to come under more scrutiny if he runs for president in 2028.

The governor, who has since married Jennifer Siebel Newsom, has been open about his interest in a possible White House bid as he has urged fellow Democrats to stand up more to President Donald Trump and "fight fire with fire."

Writing for Vanity Fair, Rippey traces the start of the affair to the summer of 2005 and said it coincided with a period in her life when she was struggling with alcohol addiction. She said she was accountable for her actions but noted that the #MeToo movement, which started in 2017, opened her eyes to the power imbalance in their relationship.

"Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly," Rippey, now sober, wrote. "For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent. For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after."

She said she considered whether to speak out publicly in the aftermath of the affair and was approached about writing a memoir. But she credited Kamala Harris, then the San Francisco district attorney, with giving her the best advice she received.

"I wouldn't say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective," she said Harris told her.

news.title: The DNC Is a Broke, Phone-Throwing Mess With a Kamala Harris Hangover
news.text:
Last week I wrote about the fact that the Democratic Party is having serious money problems. In every case you can look at, the party is way behind the fundraising of comparable groups on the Republican side of the aisle. But the situation is particularly grim for the DNC which isn't just behind in fundraising; it's actually in the red. 

The DNC ended June with $16.3 million in cash and $18.5 million in debt — putting it about $2.2 million in the red. It is a staggering hole compared to the numbers of the Republican National Committee, which held $128.5 million and reported no debt.For months, Martin and his allies have predicted that Democratic victories and the approaching midterms would bring major donors back. The midterms are now approaching. The money has not followed.

As Ed pointed out yesterday, we don't even know how bad the situation really is because the DNC has been asking vendors not to bill them until after the midterms. So there may be more debt out there that we don't know about and won't until sometime in December.

In the center of this mess is Ken Martin. Martin is apparently struggling with the failure of the DNC to the point that he is now being internally investigated for throwing a phone at someone.

Mr. Martin’s fraying nerves are showing. In a pique of frustration in early July, he threw his phone at the desk of a junior aide while upbraiding the person. The phone-tossing incident resulted in a formal complaint to the D.N.C.’s human resources department.The fallout from the phone-throwing episode was described by half a dozen people familiar with the incident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss internal party matters. None of them witnessed the encounter, and there was some dispute over how aggressively the phone was tossed. Mr. Martin was said to have thrown the phone at the desk, rather than at the aide.Mr. Martin later met with D.N.C. human resources officials about his behavior, according to three of the people.

In addition to being irrationally angry, Martin is also said to be increasingly paranoid.

Even supporters acknowledge Mr. Martin’s growing sense of paranoia. He confronted the party’s finance director this spring over what he thought was a budding coup. And before he met with the top congressional Democrats, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in mid-July, assurances were given to an ally of Mr. Martin’s that the two party leaders did not plan to use the gathering to call for the chairman’s resignation.

Martin wrote a lengthy defense of his tenure but ultimately no one can overlook the fact that the DNC is broke just months before the midterms. And that means it won't be offering any help to candidates who might need it.

For more than a decade, the D.N.C. has transferred millions of dollars every election to sister committees responsible for winning the House and Senate. But the national party is now so short on cash — even after taking out a $15 million loan last year — that officials have privately conveyed to congressional leadership that there will be no such transfers in 2026.

That $15 million taken out last year is the largest loan the DNC has ever taken out. And as NOTUS reported recently, it used its own headquarters as collateral.

The Democratic National Committee put its physical headquarters up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, according to D.C. deed records not previously reported.

How perfectly symbolic would it be if the DNC got evicted and wound up homeless. It's probably not possible. I assume someone in Hollywood would step up to rescue them before that happened. Still, the fact that they are absolutely broke three months before an election that, in many ways, ought to favor Democrats, is remarkable. Part of the problem is the Kamala Harris hangover.

Some of the problems are a hangover from 2024. While Vice President Kamala Harris raised record sums that year, her loss left many big Democratic donors disillusioned with the party. Her campaign also had millions in debt that the D.N.C. spent much of last year paying off, with Ms. Harris’s help...The single biggest expense in the Martin era was $7.3 million to buy the remnants of Ms. Harris’s campaign list from her failed 2024 bid. Ms. Harris’s political action committee used the money to cover additional remaining debts.

That's why they needed the $15 million loan last year. And they haven't recovered since then. The flood of money that Martin predicted never came. Now it's probably too late.

news.title: California Dems target AI campaign ads after Spencer Pratt and Steve Hilton’s viral political attacks
news.text:
Two California Democrats have have called on Congress to slam the brakes on Hollywood-style AI campaign ads just as they become the norm for political campaigns. 

US Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) on Monday reintroduced the “AI Ads Act,” which is seeking to ban the fraudulent use of artificial intelligence to impersonate political candidates or committees in federal campaigns as AI-generated election content becomes more sophisticated.

The push comes just days after Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton unveiled a pair of AI-generated campaign ads attacking Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra. 

One featured a riff on the “Gladiator” franchise while the other pit Hilton against a “machine” supposedly representing Democratic Party’s grip on California politics.

Those videos followed a string of viral AI videos created by the campaign of former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt. 

The ex-reality TV villain turned candidate was buoyed by the work of Los Angeles director Charles Curran, whose “Pratt Man” video riffed on the “Batman” franchise and led to millions of views.

Schiff, who originally introduced the legislation while serving in the House of Representatives, said the issue is non-partisan even if Republicans seem to have wielded AI-driven campaign videos to greater effect.

“AI-generated fraudulent advertising which uses the likeness or voices of candidates to misrepresent their positions, campaigns, or causes, or otherwise misrepresents a candidate’s point of view is not only wrong — it poses a serious threat to our democracy that should concern all Americans regardless of their party,” Schiff said.

The bill would amend the Federal Election Campaign Act to explicitly prohibit fraudulent misrepresentation through content generated wholly or partly by artificial intelligence. 

It would also broaden existing federal prohibitions by applying them to anyone falsely claiming to represent a candidate or political organization — and eliminate the requirement that a misrepresentation be shown to be “damaging” before enforcement could occur. 

The proposal closely tracks bipartisan recommendations issued by the Federal Election Commission in 2022 to modernize campaign fraud laws.

Khanna, a likely presidential candidate in 2028, said artificial intelligence should not be “used to mislead voters or undermine our democracy.”

Unlike many of the “deepfake” concerns driving lawmakers, the Hilton and Pratt videos relied on clearly fictional, stylized animation rather than realistic fabricated footage designed to appear authentic. 

The AI Ads Act targets fraudulent impersonation of candidates or political organizations, including AI-generated content used to deceive voters or solicit campaign donations under false pretenses, rather than banning AI-generated political advertising altogether.

The legislation is backed by Common Cause, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, Campaign Legal Center, Protect Democracy and Public Citizen.

More than 30 states have adopted laws addressing deceptive AI-generated election content, according to supporters of the measure, but Congress has yet to establish comparable nationwide standards for federal campaigns.

The bill’s prospects remain uncertain in a closely divided Congress, where lawmakers have repeatedly struggled to agree on broader AI regulations despite bipartisan concerns over the technology’s growing role in elections.
news.summary: Hollywood-style AI campaign ads have been proliferating across the national political landscape, leading two California Democrats to call on Congress to slam the brakes before cinematic deepfakes become the norm in American elections.
